You build what you believe your human\r\npartner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This\r\nskill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before\r\nanything gets built.\r\n\r\nPeople often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions\r\nhelp them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the\r\nhundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.\r\n\r\n## First: What Do You Actually Know?\r\n\r\nBefore you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and\r\nwhy?\r\n\r\n- **Everything that matters is in the request** (\"make the icon cornflower\r\n  blue\"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.\r\n- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.\r\n\r\nBefore you start implementing, you must, in order:\r\n\r\n1. Lay out the approaches in a message of their own, and have your\r\n   human partner pick one (see Lay out the approaches).\r\n2. Write the design doc, short or full (see Size the Work).\r\n3. Get their approval of that doc.\r\n4. Invoke the superpowers:writing-plans skill.\r\n\r\nIf nothing is open when you write your first message and there's one\r\nsensible way, steps 1 to 3 happen in that message (see Your First\r\nMessage).\r\n\r\nTwo things aren't implementing: a spike they said yes to (see Spike to\r\nfeel things out), and doing what they asked once they've opted out of\r\nthe questions.\r\n\r\n## Look Before You Ask\r\n\r\nIn an existing project, or when they've given you context (a spec, a plan,\r\na handoff, files they pointed at, earlier conversation), dig in before your\r\nfirst message. Read what they referred to and the code or material it\r\nconnects to, and keep reading until you can explain how the relevant\r\nparts work today and what this change would touch. Never ask what the\r\nproject or their context already answers, or reopen what they've\r\nalready decided.\r\n\r\n## Your First Message\r\n\r\nMove the work forward, with one of these:\r\n\r\n- **They've already said what they want** (a spec, a plan, a detailed\r\n  request): aim for about 200 words for the whole message. Echo their\r\n  request back in your own words, so they can see whether you've got its\r\n  shape: what they want, who it's for, and why, as far as they've said.\r\n  Add what you found that bears on it: how the relevant parts work today\r\n  and what the change would touch. If you found something they may not\r\n  have considered that would change what they're asking for or how it\r\n  has to be built, like a constraint, a conflict, or a cheaper path, say\r\n  so plainly. How to build it comes later, once you understand what they\r\n  want (see Lay out the approaches). End with one line inviting\r\n  corrections. Then, if they haven't told you why they want it, even if\r\n  you can guess, ask about that: one open question in their own terms,\r\n  with nothing to pick from. If they have told you, and their request\r\n  and the project leave open something whose answer would change what\r\n  gets built, ask about the one that would change it most; when its\r\n  choices can be named, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off\r\n  and which you'd pick. If nothing like that is open, there's one\r\n  sensible way: end with the short design itself (the approach, a line on\r\n  why the others don't fit, and the design in a few lines) and ask them\r\n  to approve it. Their approval covers the approach and the design: write\r\n  the short design doc as approved and go on to the plan.\r\n  Specs are often incomplete, so confirm before you build on one.\r\n- **They haven't:** one open question, in their own terms, about the\r\n  biggest thing their request leaves unsettled. Say why you're asking:\r\n  what the answer would change about what you build. For \"a website for\r\n  my bakery\": \"If it's mostly for people deciding whether to stop by,\r\n  I'd lead with hours and what's in the case today; taking orders is a\r\n  different site. What do you want someone to do when they land on it?\"\r\n\r\nHow the message ends depends on whether their message asked for\r\nbrainstorming:\r\n\r\n- **They asked for it** (by name, by invoking it, or by asking for a\r\n  design discussion): end there. They want this conversation.\r\n- **They didn't:** they may not want a conversation at all. End with a\r\n  light, one-line offer to just get going instead, like\r\n  \"Or if you'd rather I just dive in, say so.\" If they take you up on\r\n  it, this skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice\r\n  (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they\r\n  asked through the normal workflow.\r\n\r\nThat's the whole message.\r\n\r\n## The Conversation\r\n\r\nAsk a question only when the answer would change what gets built and\r\nneither the request nor the project answers it. Otherwise, state your\r\ncall and your reason as a proposal they can correct, and move the work\r\nforward. Process steps are always your calls: writing things up, where\r\nfiles go, looking further, how to show something. Do them and say so.\r\nAsk one at a time. Use plain language, pitched just a little above where\r\nyour human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use process jargon.\r\nYou never need to quote this skill to your human partner.\r\n\r\nBe clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you\r\nreport what you found, give them the most important findings and offer\r\nthe rest.\r\n\r\n**Get them describing.** Until you know why they want it, ask open\r\nquestions, with no example answers attached. Their own words carry\r\nintent that your options can't. Once you know why, when a decision has\r\nchoices you can name, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off\r\nand which you'd pick. When they say \"just guess\" or \"what do you think?\",\r\npropose something concrete.\r\n\r\n**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,\r\nmaterials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and\r\nlibraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Read from how they\r\ntalk which of those choices they want to make. Someone who raises the how\r\nor asks about trade-offs wants the options with your pick. Someone who\r\ntalks about outcomes is handing you the how: make those calls and state\r\neach in a line. When there's existing work, build on what it already\r\nuses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as\r\nsomething they agreed to.\r\n\r\n**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these\r\nout as questions:\r\n\r\n- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special\r\n- why now, and what success looks like to them\r\n- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even\r\n  if it technically works)\r\n- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated\r\n- current state: what exists now, what they've tried\r\n- the details they care about\r\n\r\n**Make every question specific** to their project and what they've told\r\nyou. Ask Socratically, the way a sharp colleague would: build each\r\nquestion on their last answer or on something you found, so it helps\r\nthem think through a consequence or a case they may have missed\r\n(\"Voting closes before the meeting, and two members joined this month.\r\nDoes someone who joins mid-round get a vote?\"). When the reason isn't\r\nalready plain, say what you're hoping to learn or what the answer would\r\nchange. A proposal they can correct, plus your reason for it, often\r\nbeats a question.\r\n\r\n**Do recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking further\r\nwould help, go look: deeper into their codebase or project, their own\r\nfiles and data, or the web. Say what you looked for and what you found.\r\n\r\n**Lay out the approaches.** Once you understand what they want, and\r\nbefore you write anything up, put the ways of building it in a message\r\nof its own. Come up with several real alternatives and drop the weak\r\nones, including any that work against why they want it and any the\r\nexisting work rules out. Sketch the two or three that remain concretely\r\nenough to picture, grounded in what the project actually does, with what\r\neach trades off. Recommend one and say why, then ask which way they want\r\nto go; if they've handed you the how, say you'll go with your pick\r\ninstead. When there's genuinely one sensible way, say so in that\r\nmessage and explain why the others don't fit; the design comes in the\r\nnext one. This is for how it gets built; for what they want, get them\r\ndescribing first.\r\n\r\n**Show, don't tell.** Whenever seeing would help more than reading,\r\nsketch it in text: a few lines of what they'd see. Offer the visual\r\ncompanion (below) when the look itself is theirs to decide:\r\n\r\n- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign\r\n- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule\r\n- a flow or a sequence of steps\r\n- options that would look different from each other\r\n- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map\r\n\r\nOnce they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side\r\noptions, and throwaway prototypes they can click.\r\n\r\n**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very\r\nfast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what\r\nthey want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.\r\nWhen they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests\r\nor minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,\r\nand review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the\r\nconversation.\r\n\r\n## Play It Back\r\n\r\nPlay back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to\r\ndescribe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece\r\nbehaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to\r\nquestions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through\r\nthe whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.\r\n\r\nOnly what they said goes in as theirs. Anything you filled in goes in\r\nas your proposal, with your reason. End each chunk by asking what's wrong\r\nor missing.\r\n\r\nBefore you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll\r\nlook at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, put a\r\ntext sketch next to the description. If the look itself is theirs to\r\ndecide and they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the\r\noffer instead (its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next\r\nmessage. Once they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.\r\n\r\n## Size the Work\r\n\r\nOnce you understand what they want and they've picked an approach, say\r\nhow big the work is in plain words. They can override it.\r\n\r\n| Size | The design doc |\r\n|------|----------------|\r\n| A small change | a short one: what you already covered together, written down |\r\n| A project | the full written design (below) |\r\n\r\nShort or full, the design doc has an **Approaches** part: the two or\r\nthree ways you considered building it, what each trades off, which one\r\nthey picked, and why. They pick in the conversation, before you write\r\nthe doc.\r\n\r\nIf it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.\r\n\r\nIf this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an\r\norder, and brainstorm them one at a time.\r\n\r\n## The Written Design\r\n\r\nWrite a plain document a talented builder in the domain could plan\r\nfrom without going back to your human partner. Cover:\r\n\r\n- intent and the why\r\n- goals, non-goals, anti-goals\r\n- constraints\r\n- approaches (above)\r\n- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them\r\n- what's left to the builder\r\n\r\nFor a small change, the short design covers the same points in a line\r\nor two each and goes straight to your human partner, without the\r\nbuilder check.\r\n\r\n**Where it goes:** in a software repo,\r\n`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.\r\nOtherwise, pick a sensible place and say where. Your human partner's\r\npreferences override both.\r\n\r\n**Builder check** (for a project): dispatch a fresh subagent with\r\n`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human\r\npartner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you\r\nmay come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document\r\nuntil the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:\r\n\r\n- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer\r\n  in the document.\r\n- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets\r\n  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.\r\n- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes\r\n  what gets built.\r\n\r\nBring the \"theirs\" pile in one message, most important first. Update the\r\ndocument with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the\r\ncalls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only\r\nround of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the\r\ndocument as that builder yourself.\r\n\r\n<HARD-GATE>\r\nNothing gets built until your human partner approves the design doc:\r\nthe short one for a small change, the full one for a project.\r\nBuilding includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing\r\ndependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.\r\nReading and exploring are fine.\r\n\r\nTwo exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done\r\nand the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it\r\nstays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request\r\nthat comes back through this gate.\r\n\r\nAfter the design doc is approved, the next step is the plan: invoke\r\nsuperpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.\r\n</HARD-GATE>\r\n\r\n## Red Flags\r\n\r\n| Thought | Reality |\r\n|---------|---------|\r\n| \"I'll offer a menu of what they might want\" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |\r\n| \"I'll fill in sensible defaults\" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |\r\n| \"I've answered their questions, so I'll write the doc\" | Lay out the approaches first, in a message of their own (or, when nothing was open from the start, in your first message's short design). |\r\n| \"I should explain the process first\" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |\r\n| \"They said 'sounds good' to the idea\" | Approval covers what you showed them. A design doc you haven't written isn't approved. |\r\n| \"The spike works, I'll keep building on it\" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |\r\n\r\n## Visual Companion\r\n\r\nA browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a\r\ntool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the\r\nbrowser.\r\n\r\n**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments\r\nabove comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing\r\nelse in it:\r\n\r\n> \"This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?\"\r\n\r\nIf they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.\r\n\r\n**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**\r\nMockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.\r\nRequirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A\r\nquestion about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.\r\n\r\nIf they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before\r\nstarting the server.\r\n---\r\nname: writing-plans\r\ndescription: Use when you have a spec or requirements for a multi-step task, before touching code\r\n---\r\n\r\n# Writing Plans\r\n\r\n## Overview\r\n\r\nWrite implementation plans for an engineer who has not seen this codebase or this spec. Assume they write idiomatic code in the project's language once they know the exact interface and the exact test, and that they will make a reasonable choice wherever the plan leaves one open. What they cannot know is what you decided: which files, which names and signatures, which values from the spec, which tests prove each task. Document those. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.\r\n\r\n**Announce at start:** \"I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan.\"\r\n\r\n**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.\r\n\r\n**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`\r\n- (User preferences for plan location override this default)\r\n\r\n## Scope Check\r\n\r\nIf the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.\r\n\r\n## File Structure\r\n\r\nBefore defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.\r\n\r\n- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.\r\n- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.\r\n- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.\r\n- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.\r\n\r\nThis structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.\r\n\r\n## Task Right-Sizing\r\n\r\nA task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a\r\nfresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,\r\nconfiguration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose\r\ndeliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully\r\nreject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an\r\nindependently testable deliverable.\r\n\r\n## Step Granularity\r\n\r\n**Each step is one action with a checkable result:**\r\n- \"Write the failing test\" - step\r\n- \"Run it to make sure it fails\" - step\r\n- \"Implement the minimal code to make the test pass\" - step\r\n- \"Run the tests and make sure they pass\" - step\r\n- \"Commit\" - step\r\n\r\n## Plan Document Header\r\n\r\n**Every plan MUST start with this header:**\r\n\r\n```markdown\r\n# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan\r\n\r\n> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.\r\n\r\n**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]\r\n\r\n**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]\r\n\r\n**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]\r\n\r\n**Spec:** [path to the spec/design doc this plan implements — the plan\r\nargues from the spec, so the spec travels with it; executors read both]\r\n\r\n## Global Constraints\r\n\r\n[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,\r\nnaming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact\r\nvalues copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly\r\ninclude this section.]\r\n\r\n## Review Focus\r\n\r\n[The five input classes or failure modes the spec implies but no task's\r\ntests exercise that are most likely to bite a person using this software\r\n— one line each, naming the input or condition and the behavior a\r\nreasonable person would expect, most likely first. The spec is a vision\r\ndocument: it says what the software must do, not everything it will\r\nmeet, and its silence on an input is not permission for that input to\r\nbreak the program. Write the list here, once, with the spec in front of\r\nyou. Then, for each line, add the test that pins it to the task that\r\nowns the code, in that task's own step style.]\r\n\r\n---\r\n```\r\n\r\n## Task Structure\r\n\r\n````markdown\r\n### Task N: [Component Name]\r\n\r\n**Files:**\r\n- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`\r\n- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`\r\n- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`\r\n\r\n**Interfaces:**\r\n- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]\r\n- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter\r\n  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this\r\n  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]\r\n\r\n- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**\r\n\r\n```python\r\ndef test_specific_behavior():\r\n    result = function(input)\r\n    assert result == expected\r\n```\r\n\r\n- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**\r\n\r\nRun: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`\r\nExpected: FAIL with \"function not defined\"\r\n\r\n- [ ] **Step 3: Implement `function(input: InputType) -> ResultType` in `exact/path/to/file.py`**\r\n\r\nOne line on the approach when the signature and the test leave a choice\r\n(which library call, which data structure); a code block only for an\r\nalgorithm they do not determine.\r\n\r\n- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**\r\n\r\nRun: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`\r\nExpected: PASS\r\n\r\n- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**\r\n\r\n```bash\r\ngit add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py\r\ngit commit -m \"feat: add specific feature\"\r\n```\r\n````\r\n\r\n## What a Step Contains\r\n\r\nA step is done when the implementer can write exactly one reasonable thing\r\nfrom it. That is the whole requirement: unambiguous, not complete. Each kind\r\nof step carries what makes it unambiguous and nothing more:\r\n\r\n- **A test step:** the test's name and its assertions, as code, with the\r\n  spec's exact values in them.\r\n- **A code step:** the exact signature (name, parameters, return type), the\r\n  file it lives in, and the specific values the spec pins. The implementer\r\n  writes the body. A body appears only for an algorithm the signature and\r\n  tests do not determine, or for exact copy the spec fixes.\r\n- **A verification step:** the command to run and the output that means it\r\n  passed.\r\n- **A reference to another task:** that task's Interfaces block says what\r\n  to use; the plan does not repeat that task's code.\r\n\r\nA plan is the set of decisions the implementer cannot make alone. A plan\r\nlonger than the code it describes has written the code instead. Lines that\r\ndecide nothing (\"TBD\", \"handle edge cases\", \"add appropriate validation\",\r\n\"write tests for the above\", a type or function no task defines) are the\r\nopposite failure, and the self-review catches both.\r\n\r\n## Self-Review\r\n\r\nAfter writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.\r\n\r\n**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.\r\n\r\n**2. Step scan:** Every step must let the implementer write exactly one reasonable thing, and no step may carry more than that: a line that decides nothing is a gap, a function body the signature and tests already determine is a transcript. Fix both.\r\n\r\n**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.\r\n\r\n**4. Review Focus:** For each input class or failure mode the spec implies, is there a task whose tests exercise it? The five uncovered ones most likely to bite a person go in the Review Focus section, and each line there gets its test added to the owning task. An empty section means you checked and found none, not that you skipped the check.\r\n\r\n**5. Proportion:** Compare the plan's length to the spec's. A plan several times longer than the spec it implements is a transcript of the program, not a plan. If code blocks are most of the document, replace bodies with signatures, test names and assertions, and check that each step is still unambiguous.\r\n\r\nIf you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.\r\n\r\n## Execution Handoff\r\n\r\nAfter saving and self-reviewing the plan, link it for your human partner\r\nto read. If they have already explicitly supplied an execution method, ask\r\nthem to review the plan and confirm it captures what they want; wait for that\r\nreview before implementation, then use the preserved method. Otherwise, ask\r\nthem to review the plan and choose an execution method before implementation.\r\n\r\n**When no execution method has already been supplied:**\r\n\r\n**\"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Which execution approach would you prefer?**\r\n\r\n- **Subagent-driven** - A fresh subagent implements each task and a fresh reviewer checks it before the next one starts, then a whole-branch review at the end. Most thorough; costs a fresh context per task and per review.\r\n- **Native** - I implement every task myself in this session, the way this harness runs work, then one fresh reviewer on the most capable model checks the whole branch. Cheapest and fastest; no independent review until the end. Runs well with a mid-tier session model, since the plan carries the design.\r\n\r\n**For this plan I recommend <one of the two>, because <one sentence from the plan: how much the tasks depend on each other's interfaces, how many there are, what a shipped mistake would cost>. Does the plan capture what you want, and which approach should we use?\"**\r\n\r\n**When an execution method has already been supplied:**\r\n\r\n**\"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Does it capture what you want?\"**\r\n\r\n**If Subagent-driven chosen:**\r\n- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development\r\n\r\n**If Native chosen:**\r\n- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans\r\n---\r\nname: test-driven-development\r\ndescription: Use when implementing any feature or bugfix, before writing implementation code\r\n---\r\n\r\n# Test-Driven Development (TDD)\r\n\r\n## Overview\r\n\r\nWrite the test first. Watch it fail. Write minimal code to pass.\r\n\r\n**Core principle:** If you didn't watch the test fail, you don't know if it tests the right thing.\r\n\r\n**Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**\r\n\r\n## When to Use\r\n\r\n**Always:**\r\n- New features\r\n- Bug fixes\r\n- Refactoring\r\n- Behavior changes\r\n\r\n**Exceptions (ask your human partner):**\r\n- Throwaway prototypes\r\n- Generated code\r\n- Configuration files\r\n\r\nThinking \"skip TDD just this once\"? Stop. That's rationalization.\r\n\r\n## The Iron Law\r\n\r\n```\r\nNO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST\r\n```\r\n\r\nWrite code before the test? Delete it. Start over.\r\n\r\n**No exceptions:**\r\n- Don't keep it as \"reference\"\r\n- Don't \"adapt\" it while writing tests\r\n- Don't look at it\r\n- Delete means delete\r\n\r\nImplement fresh from tests. Period.\r\n\r\n## Red-Green-Refactor\r\n\r\n```dot\r\ndigraph tdd_cycle {\r\n    rankdir=LR;\r\n    red [label=\"RED\\nWrite failing test\", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=\"#ffcccc\"];\r\n    verify_red [label=\"Verify fails\\ncorrectly\", shape=diamond];\r\n    green [label=\"GREEN\\nMinimal code\", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=\"#ccffcc\"];\r\n    verify_green [label=\"Verify passes\\nAll green\", shape=diamond];\r\n    refactor [label=\"REFACTOR\\nClean up\", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=\"#ccccff\"];\r\n    next [label=\"Next\", shape=ellipse];\r\n\r\n    red -> verify_red;\r\n    verify_red -> green [label=\"yes\"];\r\n    verify_red -> red [label=\"wrong\\nfailure\"];\r\n    green -> verify_green;\r\n    verify_green -> refactor [label=\"yes\"];\r\n    verify_green -> green [label=\"no\"];\r\n    refactor -> verify_green [label=\"stay\\ngreen\"];\r\n    verify_green -> next;\r\n    next -> red;\r\n}\r\n```\r\n\r\n### RED - Write Failing Test\r\n\r\nWrite one minimal test showing what should happen.\r\n\r\n<Good>\r\n```typescript\r\ntest('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {\r\n  let attempts = 0;\r\n  const operation = () => {\r\n    attempts++;\r\n    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');\r\n    return 'success';\r\n  };\r\n\r\n  const result = await retryOperation(operation);\r\n\r\n  expect(result).toBe('success');\r\n  expect(attempts).toBe(3);\r\n});\r\n```\r\nClear name, tests real behavior, one thing\r\n</Good>\r\n\r\n<Bad>\r\n```typescript\r\ntest('retry works', async () => {\r\n  const mock = jest.fn()\r\n    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())\r\n    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())\r\n    .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');\r\n  await retryOperation(mock);\r\n  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);\r\n});\r\n```\r\nVague name, tests mock not code\r\n</Bad>\r\n\r\n**Requirements:**\r\n- One behavior\r\n- Clear name\r\n- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)\r\n\r\n### Verify RED - Watch It Fail\r\n\r\n**MANDATORY. Never skip.**\r\n\r\n```bash\r\nnpm test path/to/test.test.ts\r\n```\r\n\r\nConfirm:\r\n- Test fails (not errors)\r\n- Failure message is expected\r\n- Fails because feature missing (not typos)\r\n\r\n**Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.\r\n\r\n**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.\r\n\r\n### GREEN - Minimal Code\r\n\r\nWrite simplest code to pass the test.\r\n\r\n<Good>\r\n```typescript\r\nasync function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {\r\n  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {\r\n    try {\r\n      return await fn();\r\n    } catch (e) {\r\n      if (i === 2) throw e;\r\n    }\r\n  }\r\n  throw new Error('unreachable');\r\n}\r\n```\r\nJust enough to pass\r\n</Good>\r\n\r\n<Bad>\r\n```typescript\r\nasync function retryOperation<T>(\r\n  fn: () => Promise<T>,\r\n  options?: {\r\n    maxRetries?: number;\r\n    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';\r\n    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;\r\n  }\r\n): Promise<T> {\r\n  // YAGNI\r\n}\r\n```\r\nOver-engineered\r\n</Bad>\r\n\r\nDon't add features, refactor other code, or \"improve\" beyond the test.\r\n\r\n### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass\r\n\r\n**MANDATORY.**\r\n\r\n```bash\r\nnpm test path/to/test.test.ts\r\n```\r\n\r\nConfirm:\r\n- Test passes\r\n- Other tests still pass\r\n- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)\r\n\r\n**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.\r\n\r\n**Other tests fail?** Fix now.\r\n\r\n**\"Other tests\" means the project's suite, not just your file.** A\r\ngreen run of the test you wrote is not a green suite. Before you call\r\nthe change done, run the project's test command (bare `pytest`,\r\n`npm test`, `cargo test` — whatever the repo uses) even when your task\r\nnamed only one test file. A scope statement in your task bounds the\r\ndeliverable, not your verification. Any failure that run shows —\r\nincluding one you didn't cause — goes in your report by name; a red\r\ntest you watched scroll past and didn't mention is a report falsified\r\nby omission.\r\n\r\n### REFACTOR - Clean Up\r\n\r\nAfter green only:\r\n- Remove duplication\r\n- Improve names\r\n- Extract helpers\r\n\r\nKeep tests green. Don't add behavior.\r\n\r\n### Repeat\r\n\r\nNext failing test for next feature.\r\n\r\n## Good Tests\r\n\r\n| Quality | Good | Bad |\r\n|---------|------|-----|\r\n| **Minimal** | One thing. \"and\" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |\r\n| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |\r\n| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |\r\n\r\nWhen writing or changing any test, read [writing-good-tests.md](writing-good-tests.md) for the rules that keep tests honest:\r\n- Name the production change that would make the test fail — before writing it\r\n- Assert on real behavior, never on mock behavior\r\n- Keep test-only code in test utilities, out of production classes\r\n- Understand a dependency's side effects before mocking it\r\n\r\n## Common Rationalizations\r\n\r\n| Excuse | Reality |\r\n|--------|---------|\r\n| \"Too simple to test\" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |\r\n| \"I'll test after\" | Tests written after pass immediately — which proves nothing. They may test the wrong thing, test the implementation instead of the behavior, or miss the edge case you forgot. You never watched it fail, so you never proved it can catch the bug. Test-first forces that failure. |\r\n| \"Tests after achieve same goals (spirit not ritual)\" | Tests-after answer \"what does this do?\"; tests-first answer \"what should this do?\" Tests written after are biased by the code you already wrote — you verify the cases you remembered, not the ones you'd have discovered. Coverage without proof the tests work. |\r\n| \"Already manually tested\" | Manual testing is ad-hoc: no record of what you covered, no way to re-run it when the code changes, easy to forget cases under pressure. \"Worked when I tried it\" ≠ comprehensive. Automated tests run the same way every time. |\r\n| \"Deleting X hours is wasteful\" | Sunk cost fallacy — that time is already spent either way. The real choice: rewrite with TDD (high confidence) vs. keep it and bolt tests on after (low confidence, likely bugs). Keeping code you can't trust is the waste. |\r\n| \"Keep as reference, write tests first\" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |\r\n| \"Need to explore first\" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |\r\n| \"Test hard = design unclear\" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |\r\n| \"TDD will slow me down\" | TDD IS the pragmatic path: catches bugs before commit, prevents regressions, lets you refactor without fear. \"Pragmatic\" shortcuts mean debugging in production — slower, not faster. |\r\n| \"Manual test faster\" | Manual doesn't prove edge cases. You'll re-test every change. |\r\n| \"Existing code has no tests\" | You're improving it. Add tests for existing code. |\r\n\r\n## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over\r\n\r\n- Code before test\r\n- Test after implementation\r\n- Test passes immediately\r\n- Can't explain why test failed\r\n- Tests added \"later\"\r\n- Rationalizing \"just this once\"\r\n- \"I already manually tested it\"\r\n- \"Tests after achieve the same purpose\"\r\n- \"It's about spirit not ritual\"\r\n- \"Keep as reference\" or \"adapt existing code\"\r\n- \"Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful\"\r\n- \"TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic\"\r\n- \"This is different because...\"\r\n\r\n**All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**\r\n\r\n## Example: Bug Fix\r\n\r\n**Bug:** Empty email accepted\r\n\r\n**RED**\r\n```typescript\r\ntest('rejects empty email', async () => {\r\n  const result = await submitForm({ email: '' });\r\n  expect(result.error).toBe('Email required');\r\n});\r\n```\r\n\r\n**Verify RED**\r\n```bash\r\n$ npm test\r\nFAIL: expected 'Email required', got undefined\r\n```\r\n\r\n**GREEN**\r\n```typescript\r\nfunction submitForm(data: FormData) {\r\n  if (!data.email?.trim()) {\r\n    return { error: 'Email required' };\r\n  }\r\n  // ...\r\n}\r\n```\r\n\r\n**Verify GREEN**\r\n```bash\r\n$ npm test\r\nPASS\r\n```\r\n\r\n**REFACTOR**\r\nExtract validation for multiple fields if needed.\r\n\r\n## Verification Checklist\r\n\r\nBefore marking work complete:\r\n\r\n- [ ] Every new function/method has a test\r\n- [ ] Watched each test fail before implementing\r\n- [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)\r\n- [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test\r\n- [ ] All tests pass\r\n- [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)\r\n- [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)\r\n- [ ] Edge cases and errors covered\r\n\r\nCan't check all boxes? You skipped TDD. Start over.\r\n\r\n## When Stuck\r\n\r\n| Problem | Solution |\r\n|---------|----------|\r\n| Don't know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |\r\n| Test too complicated | Design too complicated. Simplify interface. |\r\n| Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |\r\n| Test setup huge | Extract helpers. Still complex? Simplify design. |\r\n\r\n## Debugging Integration\r\n\r\nBug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.\r\n\r\nNever fix bugs without a test.\r\n\r\n## Final Rule\r\n\r\n```\r\nProduction code → test exists and failed first\r\nOtherwise → not TDD\r\n```\r\n\r\nNo exceptions without your human partner's permission.\r\n---\r\nname: systematic-debugging\r\ndescription: Use when encountering any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior, before proposing fixes\r\n---\r\n\r\n# Systematic Debugging\r\n\r\n## Overview\r\n\r\n**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.\r\n\r\n**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**\r\n\r\n## The Iron Law\r\n\r\n```\r\nNO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST\r\n```\r\n\r\nIf you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.\r\n\r\n## When to Use\r\n\r\nUse for ANY technical issue:\r\n- Test failures\r\n- Bugs in production\r\n- Unexpected behavior\r\n- Performance problems\r\n- Build failures\r\n- Integration issues\r\n\r\n**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**\r\n- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)\r\n- \"Just one quick fix\" seems obvious\r\n- You've already tried multiple fixes\r\n- Previous fix didn't work\r\n- You don't fully understand the issue\r\n\r\n**Don't skip when:**\r\n- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)\r\n- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)\r\n- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)\r\n\r\n## The Four Phases\r\n\r\nYou MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.\r\n\r\n### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation\r\n\r\n**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**\r\n\r\n1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**\r\n   - Don't skip past errors or warnings\r\n   - They often contain the exact solution\r\n   - Read stack traces completely\r\n   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes\r\n\r\n2. **Reproduce Consistently**\r\n   - Can you trigger it reliably?\r\n   - What are the exact steps?\r\n   - Does it happen every time?\r\n   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess\r\n\r\n3. **Check Recent Changes**\r\n   - What changed that could cause this?\r\n   - Git diff, recent commits\r\n   - New dependencies, config changes\r\n   - Environmental differences\r\n\r\n4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**\r\n\r\n   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**\r\n\r\n   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**\r\n   ```\r\n   For EACH component boundary:\r\n     - Log what data enters component\r\n     - Log what data exits component\r\n     - Verify environment/config propagation\r\n     - Check state at each layer\r\n\r\n   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks\r\n   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component\r\n   THEN investigate that specific component\r\n   ```\r\n\r\n   **Example (multi-layer system):**\r\n   ```bash\r\n   # Layer 1: Workflow\r\n   echo \"=== Secrets available in workflow: ===\"\r\n   echo \"IDENTITY: $([ -n \"${IDENTITY:-}\" ] && echo SET || echo UNSET)\"\r\n\r\n   # Layer 2: Build script\r\n   echo \"=== Env vars in build script: ===\"\r\n   printenv IDENTITY >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo \"IDENTITY in environment\" || echo \"IDENTITY not in environment\"\r\n\r\n   # Layer 3: Signing script\r\n   echo \"=== Keychain state: ===\"\r\n   security list-keychains\r\n   security find-identity -v\r\n\r\n   # Layer 4: Actual signing\r\n   codesign --sign \"$IDENTITY\" --verbose=4 \"$APP\"\r\n   ```\r\n\r\n   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)\r\n\r\n5. **Trace Data Flow**\r\n\r\n   **WHEN error is deep in call stack:**\r\n\r\n   See `root-cause-tracing.md` in this directory for the complete backward tracing technique.\r\n\r\n   **Quick version:**\r\n   - Where does bad value originate?\r\n   - What called this with bad value?\r\n   - Keep tracing up until you find the source\r\n   - Fix at source, not at symptom\r\n\r\n### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis\r\n\r\n**Find the pattern before fixing:**\r\n\r\n1. **Find Working Examples**\r\n   - Locate similar working code in same codebase\r\n   - What works that's similar to what's broken?\r\n\r\n2. **Compare Against References**\r\n   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY\r\n   - Don't skim - read every line\r\n   - Understand the pattern fully before applying\r\n\r\n3. **Identify Differences**\r\n   - What's different between working and broken?\r\n   - List every difference, however small\r\n   - Don't assume \"that can't matter\"\r\n\r\n4. **Understand Dependencies**\r\n   - What other components does this need?\r\n   - What settings, config, environment?\r\n   - What assumptions does it make?\r\n\r\n### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing\r\n\r\n**Scientific method:**\r\n\r\n1. **Form Single Hypothesis**\r\n   - State clearly: \"I think X is the root cause because Y\"\r\n   - Write it down\r\n   - Be specific, not vague\r\n\r\n2. **Test Minimally**\r\n   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis\r\n   - One variable at a time\r\n   - Don't fix multiple things at once\r\n\r\n3. **Verify Before Continuing**\r\n   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4\r\n   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis\r\n   - DON'T add more fixes on top\r\n\r\n4. **When You Don't Know**\r\n   - Say \"I don't understand X\"\r\n   - Don't pretend to know\r\n   - Ask for help\r\n   - Research more\r\n\r\n### Phase 4: Implementation\r\n\r\n**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**\r\n\r\n1. **Create Failing Test Case**\r\n   - Simplest possible reproduction\r\n   - Automated test if possible\r\n   - One-off test script if no framework\r\n   - MUST have before fixing\r\n   - Use the `superpowers:test-driven-development` skill for writing proper failing tests\r\n\r\n2. **Implement Single Fix**\r\n   - Address the root cause identified\r\n   - ONE change at a time\r\n   - No \"while I'm here\" improvements\r\n   - No bundled refactoring\r\n\r\n3. **Verify Fix**\r\n   - Test passes now?\r\n   - No other tests broken?\r\n   - Issue actually resolved?\r\n   - Use the `superpowers:verification-before-completion` skill before claiming success\r\n\r\n4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**\r\n   - STOP\r\n   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?\r\n   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information\r\n   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**\r\n   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion\r\n\r\n5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**\r\n\r\n   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**\r\n   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place\r\n   - Fixes require \"massive refactoring\" to implement\r\n   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere\r\n\r\n   **STOP and question fundamentals:**\r\n   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?\r\n   - Are we \"sticking with it through sheer inertia\"?\r\n   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?\r\n\r\n   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**\r\n\r\n   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.\r\n\r\n## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process\r\n\r\nIf you catch yourself thinking:\r\n- \"Quick fix for now, investigate later\"\r\n- \"Just try changing X and see if it works\"\r\n- \"Add multiple changes, run tests\"\r\n- \"Skip the test, I'll manually verify\"\r\n- \"It's probably X, let me fix that\"\r\n- \"I don't fully understand but this might work\"\r\n- \"Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently\"\r\n- \"Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]\"\r\n- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow\r\n- **\"One more fix attempt\" (when already tried 2+)**\r\n- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**\r\n\r\n**ALL of these mean: STOP. Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |\\r\\n| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |\\r\\n| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen writing or changing any test, read [writing-good-tests.md](writing-good-tests.md) for the rules that keep tests honest:\\r\\n- Name the production change that would make the test fail — before writing it\\r\\n- Assert on real behavior, never on mock behavior\\r\\n- Keep test-only code in test utilities, out of production classes\\r\\n- Understand a dependency's side effects before mocking it\\r\\n\\r\\n## Common Rationalizations\\r\\n\\r\\n| Excuse | Reality |\\r\\n|--------|---------|\\r\\n| \\\"Too simple to test\\\" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |\\r\\n| \\\"I'll test after\\\" | Tests written after pass immediately — which proves nothing. They may test the wrong thing, test the implementation instead of the behavior, or miss the edge case you forgot. You never watched it fail, so you never proved it can catch the bug. Test-first forces that failure. |\\r\\n| \\\"Tests after achieve same goals (spirit not ritual)\\\" | Tests-after answer \\\"what does this do?\\\"; tests-first answer \\\"what should this do?\\\" Tests written after are biased by the code you already wrote — you verify the cases you remembered, not the ones you'd have discovered. Coverage without proof the tests work. |\\r\\n| \\\"Already manually tested\\\" | Manual testing is ad-hoc: no record of what you covered, no way to re-run it when the code changes, easy to forget cases under pressure. \\\"Worked when I tried it\\\" ≠ comprehensive. Automated tests run the same way every time. |\\r\\n| \\\"Deleting X hours is wasteful\\\" | Sunk cost fallacy — that time is already spent either way. The real choice: rewrite with TDD (high confidence) vs. keep it and bolt tests on after (low confidence, likely bugs). Keeping code you can't trust is the waste. |\\r\\n| \\\"Keep as reference, write tests first\\\" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |\\r\\n| \\\"Need to explore first\\\" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |\\r\\n| \\\"Test hard = design unclear\\\" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |\\r\\n| \\\"TDD will slow me down\\\" | TDD IS the pragmatic path: catches bugs before commit, prevents regressions, lets you refactor without fear. \\\"Pragmatic\\\" shortcuts mean debugging in production — slower, not faster. |\\r\\n| \\\"Manual test faster\\\" | Manual doesn't prove edge cases. You'll re-test every change. |\\r\\n| \\\"Existing code has no tests\\\" | You're improving it. Add tests for existing code. |\\r\\n\\r\\n## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over\\r\\n\\r\\n- Code before test\\r\\n- Test after implementation\\r\\n- Test passes immediately\\r\\n- Can't explain why test failed\\r\\n- Tests added \\\"later\\\"\\r\\n- Rationalizing \\\"just this once\\\"\\r\\n- \\\"I already manually tested it\\\"\\r\\n- \\\"Tests after achieve the same purpose\\\"\\r\\n- \\\"It's about spirit not ritual\\\"\\r\\n- \\\"Keep as reference\\\" or \\\"adapt existing code\\\"\\r\\n- \\\"Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful\\\"\\r\\n- \\\"TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic\\\"\\r\\n- \\\"This is different because...\\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n**All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**\\r\\n\\r\\n## Example: Bug Fix\\r\\n\\r\\n**Bug:** Empty email accepted\\r\\n\\r\\n**RED**\\r\\n```typescript\\r\\ntest('rejects empty email', async () => {\\r\\n  const result = await submitForm({ email: '' });\\r\\n  expect(result.error).toBe('Email required');\\r\\n});\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**Verify RED**\\r\\n```bash\\r\\n$ npm test\\r\\nFAIL: expected 'Email required', got undefined\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**GREEN**\\r\\n```typescript\\r\\nfunction submitForm(data: FormData) {\\r\\n  if (!data.email?.trim()) {\\r\\n    return { error: 'Email required' };\\r\\n  }\\r\\n  // ...\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**Verify GREEN**\\r\\n```bash\\r\\n$ npm test\\r\\nPASS\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**REFACTOR**\\r\\nExtract validation for multiple fields if needed.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Verification Checklist\\r\\n\\r\\nBefore marking work complete:\\r\\n\\r\\n- [ ] Every new function/method has a test\\r\\n- [ ] Watched each test fail before implementing\\r\\n- [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)\\r\\n- [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test\\r\\n- [ ] All tests pass\\r\\n- [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)\\r\\n- [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)\\r\\n- [ ] Edge cases and errors covered\\r\\n\\r\\nCan't check all boxes? You skipped TDD. Start over.\\r\\n\\r\\n## When Stuck\\r\\n\\r\\n| Problem | Solution |\\r\\n|---------|----------|\\r\\n| Don't know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |\\r\\n| Test too complicated | Design too complicated. Simplify interface. |\\r\\n| Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |\\r\\n| Test setup huge | Extract helpers. Still complex? Simplify design. |\\r\\n\\r\\n## Debugging Integration\\r\\n\\r\\nBug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.\\r\\n\\r\\nNever fix bugs without a test.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Final Rule\\r\\n\\r\\n```\\r\\nProduction code → test exists and failed first\\r\\nOtherwise → not TDD\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nNo exceptions without your human partner's permission.\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: systematic-debugging\\r\\ndescription: Use when encountering any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior, before proposing fixes\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Systematic Debugging\\r\\n\\r\\n## Overview\\r\\n\\r\\n**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**\\r\\n\\r\\n## The Iron Law\\r\\n\\r\\n```\\r\\nNO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nIf you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.\\r\\n\\r\\n## When to Use\\r\\n\\r\\nUse for ANY technical issue:\\r\\n- Test failures\\r\\n- Bugs in production\\r\\n- Unexpected behavior\\r\\n- Performance problems\\r\\n- Build failures\\r\\n- Integration issues\\r\\n\\r\\n**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**\\r\\n- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)\\r\\n- \\\"Just one quick fix\\\" seems obvious\\r\\n- You've already tried multiple fixes\\r\\n- Previous fix didn't work\\r\\n- You don't fully understand the issue\\r\\n\\r\\n**Don't skip when:**\\r\\n- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)\\r\\n- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)\\r\\n- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)\\r\\n\\r\\n## The Four Phases\\r\\n\\r\\nYou MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation\\r\\n\\r\\n**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**\\r\\n   - Don't skip past errors or warnings\\r\\n   - They often contain the exact solution\\r\\n   - Read stack traces completely\\r\\n   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes\\r\\n\\r\\n2. **Reproduce Consistently**\\r\\n   - Can you trigger it reliably?\\r\\n   - What are the exact steps?\\r\\n   - Does it happen every time?\\r\\n   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess\\r\\n\\r\\n3. **Check Recent Changes**\\r\\n   - What changed that could cause this?\\r\\n   - Git diff, recent commits\\r\\n   - New dependencies, config changes\\r\\n   - Environmental differences\\r\\n\\r\\n4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**\\r\\n\\r\\n   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**\\r\\n\\r\\n   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**\\r\\n   ```\\r\\n   For EACH component boundary:\\r\\n     - Log what data enters component\\r\\n     - Log what data exits component\\r\\n     - Verify environment/config propagation\\r\\n     - Check state at each layer\\r\\n\\r\\n   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks\\r\\n   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component\\r\\n   THEN investigate that specific component\\r\\n   ```\\r\\n\\r\\n   **Example (multi-layer system):**\\r\\n   ```bash\\r\\n   # Layer 1: Workflow\\r\\n   echo \\\"=== Secrets available in workflow: ===\\\"\\r\\n   echo \\\"IDENTITY: $([ -n \\\"${IDENTITY:-}\\\" ] && echo SET || echo UNSET)\\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n   # Layer 2: Build script\\r\\n   echo \\\"=== Env vars in build script: ===\\\"\\r\\n   printenv IDENTITY >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo \\\"IDENTITY in environment\\\" || echo \\\"IDENTITY not in environment\\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n   # Layer 3: Signing script\\r\\n   echo \\\"=== Keychain state: ===\\\"\\r\\n   security list-keychains\\r\\n   security find-identity -v\\r\\n\\r\\n   # Layer 4: Actual signing\\r\\n   codesign --sign \\\"$IDENTITY\\\" --verbose=4 \\\"$APP\\\"\\r\\n   ```\\r\\n\\r\\n   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)\\r\\n\\r\\n5. **Trace Data Flow**\\r\\n\\r\\n   **WHEN error is deep in call stack:**\\r\\n\\r\\n   See `root-cause-tracing.md` in this directory for the complete backward tracing technique.\\r\\n\\r\\n   **Quick version:**\\r\\n   - Where does bad value originate?\\r\\n   - What called this with bad value?\\r\\n   - Keep tracing up until you find the source\\r\\n   - Fix at source, not at symptom\\r\\n\\r\\n### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis\\r\\n\\r\\n**Find the pattern before fixing:**\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Find Working Examples**\\r\\n   - Locate similar working code in same codebase\\r\\n   - What works that's similar to what's broken?\\r\\n\\r\\n2. **Compare Against References**\\r\\n   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY\\r\\n   - Don't skim - read every line\\r\\n   - Understand the pattern fully before applying\\r\\n\\r\\n3. **Identify Differences**\\r\\n   - What's different between working and broken?\\r\\n   - List every difference, however small\\r\\n   - Don't assume \\\"that can't matter\\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n4. **Understand Dependencies**\\r\\n   - What other components does this need?\\r\\n   - What settings, config, environment?\\r\\n   - What assumptions does it make?\\r\\n\\r\\n### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing\\r\\n\\r\\n**Scientific method:**\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Form Single Hypothesis**\\r\\n   - State clearly: \\\"I think X is the root cause because Y\\\"\\r\\n   - Write it down\\r\\n   - Be specific, not vague\\r\\n\\r\\n2. **Test Minimally**\\r\\n   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis\\r\\n   - One variable at a time\\r\\n   - Don't fix multiple things at once\\r\\n\\r\\n3. **Verify Before Continuing**\\r\\n   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4\\r\\n   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis\\r\\n   - DON'T add more fixes on top\\r\\n\\r\\n4. **When You Don't Know**\\r\\n   - Say \\\"I don't understand X\\\"\\r\\n   - Don't pretend to know\\r\\n   - Ask for help\\r\\n   - Research more\\r\\n\\r\\n### Phase 4: Implementation\\r\\n\\r\\n**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Create Failing Test Case**\\r\\n   - Simplest possible reproduction\\r\\n   - Automated test if possible\\r\\n   - One-off test script if no framework\\r\\n   - MUST have before fixing\\r\\n   - Use the `superpowers:test-driven-development` skill for writing proper failing tests\\r\\n\\r\\n2. **Implement Single Fix**\\r\\n   - Address the root cause identified\\r\\n   - ONE change at a time\\r\\n   - No \\\"while I'm here\\\" improvements\\r\\n   - No bundled refactoring\\r\\n\\r\\n3. **Verify Fix**\\r\\n   - Test passes now?\\r\\n   - No other tests broken?\\r\\n   - Issue actually resolved?\\r\\n   - Use the `superpowers:verification-before-completion` skill before claiming success\\r\\n\\r\\n4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**\\r\\n   - STOP\\r\\n   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?\\r\\n   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information\\r\\n   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**\\r\\n   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion\\r\\n\\r\\n5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**\\r\\n\\r\\n   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**\\r\\n   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place\\r\\n   - Fixes require \\\"massive refactoring\\\" to implement\\r\\n   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere\\r\\n\\r\\n   **STOP and question fundamentals:**\\r\\n   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?\\r\\n   - Are we \\\"sticking with it through sheer inertia\\\"?\\r\\n   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?\\r\\n\\r\\n   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**\\r\\n\\r\\n   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process\\r\\n\\r\\nIf you catch yourself thinking:\\r\\n- \\\"Quick fix for now, investigate later\\\"\\r\\n- \\\"Just try changing X and see if it works\\\"\\r\\n- \\\"Add multiple changes, run tests\\\"\\r\\n- \\\"Skip the test, I'll manually verify\\\"\\r\\n- \\\"It's probably X, let me fix that\\\"\\r\\n- \\\"I don't fully understand but this might work\\\"\\r\\n- \\\"Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently\\\"\\r\\n- \\\"Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]\\\"\\r\\n- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow\\r\\n- **\\\"One more fix attempt\\\" (when already tried 2+)**\\r\\n- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**\\r\\n\\r\\n**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**\\r\\n\\r\\n**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)\\r\\n\\r\\n## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong\\r\\n\\r\\n**Watch for these redirections:**\\r\\n- \\\"Is that not happening?\\\" - You assumed without verifying\\r\\n- \\\"Will it show us...?\\\" - You should have added evidence gathering\\r\\n- \\\"Stop guessing\\\" - You're proposing fixes without understanding\\r\\n- \\\"Ultra-think this\\\" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms\\r\\n- \\\"We're stuck?\\\" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working\\r\\n\\r\\n**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Common Rationalizations\\r\\n\\r\\n| Excuse | Reality |\\r\\n|--------|---------|\\r\\n| \\\"Issue is simple, don't need process\\\" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |\\r\\n| \\\"Emergency, no time for process\\\" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |\\r\\n| \\\"Just try this first, then investigate\\\" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |\\r\\n| \\\"I'll write test after confirming fix works\\\" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |\\r\\n| \\\"Multiple fixes at once saves time\\\" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |\\r\\n| \\\"Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern\\\" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |\\r\\n| \\\"I see the problem, let me fix it\\\" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |\\r\\n| \\\"One more fix attempt\\\" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |\\r\\n\\r\\n## Quick Reference\\r\\n\\r\\n| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |\\r\\n|-------|---------------|------------------|\\r\\n| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |\\r\\n| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |\\r\\n| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |\\r\\n| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |\\r\\n\\r\\n## When Process Reveals \\\"No Root Cause\\\"\\r\\n\\r\\nIf systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. On this run, **all 114 tests ran and passed, with no skips**.\r\n\r\nThe RLS trust boundary is explicit:\r\n\r\n1. `SupabaseJWTVerifier` fetches keys only from the configured project's HTTPS `/auth/v1/.well-known/jwks.json`. It verifies ES256/RS256 signatures, expiration, issued-at, optional not-before, exact issuer, audience, UUID subject, and `role = authenticated`. Missing claims, unknown keys, wrong signatures, and unsupported algorithms fail closed. Token-provided key URLs and user IDs from request bodies are not trusted.\r\n2. `Database.user_session(token, verifier)` verifies before acquiring a connection. The runtime login must inherit authenticated, lack superuser/BYPASSRLS/role-creation/database-creation privileges and privileged memberships, and have no ownership path to the four tables. It must connect as itself; an admin connection followed by role impersonation is rejected.\r\n3. One SQLAlchemy transaction sets only the verified UUID and fixed authenticated role through parameterized `set_config(..., true)` calls. Both modern `request.jwt.claims` and legacy claim settings are overwritten. These settings are transaction-local. All reads/writes occur inside that transaction. `session.info['user_id']` is the verified owner to use when constructing future records.\r\n4. RLS checks existing ownership with USING and proposed ownership with WITH CHECK. Column grants additionally prohibit changing owner keys, generated IDs, timestamps, and source/status constants. Profiles and preferences cannot be directly deleted by clients; preferences cannot be directly inserted. The profile trigger creates the child atomically.\r\n5. Commit or rollback removes identity before pool reuse. The tests deliberately use a pool of size one, assert the same PostgreSQL backend PID is reused, check two distinct users, and then verify that unscoped auth.uid() is NULL after both success and failure.\r\n\r\nThe runtime database credential remains a **trusted backend secret**. Anyone holding raw database credentials could issue their own custom claim settings; PostgreSQL is not independently verifying a JWT inside auth.uid(). Do not give SQL access or the runtime password to Flutter/end users, and do not accept arbitrary SQL from clients. The supplied FastAPI dependency obtains a bearer token from the Authorization header and uses this verified transaction mechanism; it defines no API routes. Keep ORM owner filters in future services as an additional check.\r\n\r\nJWT verification currently supports asymmetric Supabase signing keys only. A project still using legacy HS256 will fail authentication rather than using an unverified fallback or sharing its JWT secret with clients. Such a project needs an approved signing-key change or a separately reviewed server-side Auth verification method before protected operations are enabled. The remote project's signing keys have not been inspected.\r\n\r\nWeekly events persist local dates/times, an explicit end-day offset and their own IANA timezone. ONCE and WEEKLY shapes are mutually exclusive. Database triggers validate timezone names; Python helpers validate a name or a single local endpoint and reject DST gaps/folds. There is no recurrence expansion engine, occurrence table, holiday exception model, or optimization. Future occurrence resolution must validate both endpoints and positive resolved duration using current timezone data; row checks cannot prove all future DST outcomes. A preference timezone change does not rewrite existing event rules.\r\n\r\nRuntime and migration URLs are independent:\r\n\r\n| Variable | Purpose |\r\n|---|---|\r\n| DATABASE_URL | Restricted backend PostgreSQL login used by engine/session/check code. |\r\n| MIGRATION_DATABASE_URL | Separate trusted migration/admin login; no fallback to DATABASE_URL. |\r\n| SUPABASE_URL | Trusted HTTPS project origin for JWT verification, required when enabling protected sessions. |\r\n| SUPABASE_JWT_AUDIENCE | Must be authenticated. |\r\n| TEST_DATABASE_ADMIN_URL | Optional loopback-only admin URL for disposable automated tests. |\r\n| PG_BIN | Optional path to local PostgreSQL binaries. |\r\n\r\nPasswords must be URL-encoded in URLs. `.env`, `.local`, and virtual environments are ignored. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.\r\n\r\n## File Structure\r\n\r\nBefore defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.\r\n\r\n- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.\r\n- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.\r\n- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.\r\n- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.\r\n\r\nThis structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.\r\n\r\n## Task Right-Sizing\r\n\r\nA task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a\r\nfresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,\r\nconfiguration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose\r\ndeliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully\r\nreject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an\r\nindependently testable deliverable.\r\n\r\n## Step Granularity\r\n\r\n**Each step is one action with a checkable result:**\r\n- \"Write the failing test\" - step\r\n- \"Run it to make sure it fails\" - step\r\n- \"Implement the minimal code to make the test pass\" - step\r\n- \"Run the tests and make sure they pass\" - step\r\n- \"Commit\" - step\r\n\r\n## Plan Document Header\r\n\r\n**Every plan MUST start with this header:**\r\n\r\n```markdown\r\n# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan\r\n\r\n> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.\r\n\r\n**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]\r\n\r\n**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]\r\n\r\n**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]\r\n\r\n**Spec:** [path to the spec/design doc this plan implements — the plan\r\nargues from the spec, so the spec travels with it; executors read both]\r\n\r\n## Global Constraints\r\n\r\n[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,\r\nnaming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact\r\nvalues copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly\r\ninclude this section.]\r\n\r\n## Review Focus\r\n\r\n[The five input classes or failure modes the spec implies but no task's\r\ntests exercise that are most likely to bite a person using this software\r\n— one line each, naming the input or condition and the behavior a\r\nreasonable person would expect, most likely first. The spec is a vision\r\ndocument: it says what the software must do, not everything it will\r\nmeet, and its silence on an input is not permission for that input to\r\nbreak the program. Write the list here, once, with the spec in front of\r\nyou. Then, for each line, add the test that pins it to the task that\r\nowns the code, in that task's own step style.]\r\n\r\n---\r\n```\r\n\r\n## Task Structure\r\n\r\n````markdown\r\n### Task N: [Component Name]\r\n\r\n**Files:**\r\n- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`\r\n- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`\r\n- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`\r\n\r\n**Interfaces:**\r\n- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]\r\n- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter\r\n  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this\r\n  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]\r\n\r\n- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**\r\n\r\n```python\r\ndef test_specific_behavior():\r\n    result = function(input)\r\n    assert result == expected\r\n```\r\n\r\n- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**\r\n\r\nRun: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`\r\nExpected: FAIL with \"function not defined\"\r\n\r\n- [ ] **Step 3: Implement `function(input: InputType) -> ResultType` in `exact/path/to/file.py`**\r\n\r\nOne line on the approach when the signature and the test leave a choice\r\n(which library call, which data structure); a code block only for an\r\nalgorithm they do not determine.\r\n\r\n- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**\r\n\r\nRun: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`\r\nExpected: PASS\r\n\r\n- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**\r\n\r\n```bash\r\ngit add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py\r\ngit commit -m \"feat: add specific feature\"\r\n```\r\n````\r\n\r\n## What a Step Contains\r\n\r\nA step is done when the implementer can write exactly one reasonable thing\r\nfrom it. That is the whole requirement: unambiguous, not complete. Each kind\r\nof step carries what makes it unambiguous and nothing more:\r\n\r\n- **A test step:** the test's name and its assertions, as code, with the\r\n  spec's exact values in them.\r\n- **A code step:** the exact signature (name, parameters, return type), the\r\n  file it lives in, and the specific values the spec pins. The implementer\r\n  writes the body. A body appears only for an algorithm the signature and\r\n  tests do not determine, or for exact copy the spec fixes.\r\n- **A verification step:** the command to run and the output that means it\r\n  passed.\r\n- **A reference to another task:** that task's Interfaces block says what\r\n  to use; the plan does not repeat that task's code.\r\n\r\nA plan is the set of decisions the implementer cannot make alone. A plan\r\nlonger than the code it describes has written the code instead. Lines that\r\ndecide nothing (\"TBD\", \"handle edge cases\", \"add appropriate validation\",\r\n\"write tests for the above\", a type or function no task defines) are the\r\nopposite failure, and the self-review catches both.\r\n\r\n## Self-Review\r\n\r\nAfter writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.\r\n\r\n**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.\r\n\r\n**2. Step scan:** Every step must let the implementer write exactly one reasonable thing, and no step may carry more than that: a line that decides nothing is a gap, a function body the signature and tests already determine is a transcript. Fix both.\r\n\r\n**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.\r\n\r\n**4. Review Focus:** For each input class or failure mode the spec implies, is there a task whose tests exercise it? The five uncovered ones most likely to bite a person go in the Review Focus section, and each line there gets its test added to the owning task. An empty section means you checked and found none, not that you skipped the check.\r\n\r\n**5. Proportion:** Compare the plan's length to the spec's. A plan several times longer than the spec it implements is a transcript of the program, not a plan. If code blocks are most of the document, replace bodies with signatures, test names and assertions, and check that each step is still unambiguous.\r\n\r\nIf you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.\r\n\r\n## Execution Handoff\r\n\r\nAfter saving and self-reviewing the plan, link it for your human partner\r\nto read. If they have already explicitly supplied an execution method, ask\r\nthem to review the plan and confirm it captures what they want; wait for that\r\nreview before implementation, then use the preserved method. Otherwise, ask\r\nthem to review the plan and choose an execution method before implementation.\r\n\r\n**When no execution method has already been supplied:**\r\n\r\n**\"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Which execution approach would you prefer?**\r\n\r\n- **Subagent-driven** - A fresh subagent implements each task and a fresh reviewer checks it before the next one starts, then a whole-branch review at the end. Most thorough; costs a fresh context per task and per review.\r\n- **Native** - I implement every task myself in this session, the way this harness runs work, then one fresh reviewer on the most capable model checks the whole branch. Cheapest and fastest; no independent review until the end. Runs well with a mid-tier session model, since the plan carries the design.\r\n\r\n**For this plan I recommend <one of the two>, because <one sentence from the plan: how much the tasks depend on each other's interfaces, how many there are, what a shipped mistake would cost>.
