postgres-15-19-17-11-breaking-changes\\npublished: 2026-09-25\\nchange_type: breaking-change\\naffected_products:\\n  - Database\\npage: https://supabase.com/changelog/postgres-15-19-17-11-breaking-changes\\n---\\n\\n# PostgreSQL 15.19 / 17.11 minor release — action may be required for ltree, pgcrypto, btree_gist, and custom operators\\n\\n## What changed\\n\\nWe are rolling out the PostgreSQL **15.19 / 17.11** minor release (from 15.14 / 17.6).\\nIt bundles five upstream security cycles and closes **44 CVEs**.\\nFour changes may require action, depending on how you use your database:\\n\\n1. **ltree indexes may need reindexing** — a case-folding fix on multibyte/ICU databases, plus an integer-overflow fix for very deep `ltree` values (any encoding).\\n2. **pgcrypto stops decrypting legacy-cipher PGP data** (CVE-2026-14663) — data encrypted with `cipher-algo=bf`/`blowfish`/`cast5` was effectively stored unencrypted and fails to decrypt by default after the upgrade.\\n3. **btree_gist indexes on float columns** that may contain `NaN` need reindexing.\\n4. **Custom operators with non-built-in selectivity estimators** (CVE-2026-2004) — recreating them (dump/restore, branching) now requires superuser.\\n\\nIf none of the detection queries below return rows for your project, no action is needed.\\n\\n## Why we made this change\\n\\nThis is an upstream PostgreSQL minor release.\\nStaying current closes 44 CVEs (including several rated High) and picks up correctness fixes in the `ltree` and `btree_gist` extensions.\\n\\n## Who is affected\\n\\n### 1. ltree indexes\\n\\n#### Case-folding (multibyte/ICU)\\n\\nAfter upgrading, indexes on `ltree` columns built under the previous version can silently return incomplete results on databases using a multibyte encoding (such as UTF-8) or a non-`libc` collation provider (ICU or builtin).\\nCheck whether your database is affected:\\n\\n```sql\\nselect\\n  pg_encoding_to_char(encoding) as encoding,\\n  pg_encoding_max_length(encoding) as max_bytes_per_char, -- 1 = single-byte, >1 = multibyte\\n  datlocprovider as collation_provider, -- 'c' libc, 'i' icu, 'b' builtin\\n  (pg_encoding_max_length(encoding) > 1 or datlocprovider != 'c') as reindex_required\\nfrom pg_database\\nwhere datname = current_database();\\n```\\n\\nIf `reindex_required` is `true`, find the affected indexes:\\n\\n```sql\\nselect distinct\\n  n.nspname as schema_name,\\n  cls.relname as table_name,\\n  ic.relname as index_name\\nfrom pg_index idx\\n  join pg_class ic on idx.indexrelid = ic.oid\\n  join pg_class cls on idx.indrelid = cls.oid\\n  join pg_namespace n on ic.relnamespace = n.oid\\n  join lateral unnest(idx.indclass::oid[]) with ordinality as k(opclass, pos) on true\\n  join pg_opclass oc on oc.oid = k.opclass\\n  join pg_type ty on ty.oid = oc.opcintype\\nwhere\\n  k.pos <= idx.indnkeyatts -- key columns only, excludes INCLUDE\\n  and ty.typname in ('ltree', '_ltree');\\n```\\n\\n#### Integer overflow (any encoding)\\n\\nThis release also fixes an integer overflow in `ltree` comparisons: values with more than about 14,653 labels could compare incorrectly, which can corrupt B-tree indexes built over them, regardless of your database encoding.\\nThis query lists only the B-tree indexes that actually contain such values (an empty result means no action is needed):\\n\\n```sql\\nselect s.schema_name || '.' || s.index_name as index_to_reindex\\nfrom (\\n  select\\n    n.nspname as schema_name,\\n    c.relname as table_name,\\n    ic.relname as index_name,\\n    min(pg_get_expr(i.indpred, i.indrelid)) as pred, -- partial-index predicate, if any\\n    string_agg('nlevel(' || pg_get_indexdef(i.indexrelid, k.pos::int, true) || ') > 14653', ' or ') as keys_cond\\n  from pg_index i\\n  join pg_class ic on ic.oid = i.indexrelid\\n  join pg_class c on c.oid = i.indrelid\\n  join pg_namespace n on n.oid = c.relnamespace\\n  join pg_am am on am.oid = ic.relam\\n  join lateral generate_series(1, i.indnkeyatts) as k(pos) on true\\n  join pg_attribute ia on ia.attrelid = i.indexrelid and ia.attnum = k.pos\\n  join pg_type t on t.oid = ia.atttypid\\n  where am.amname = 'btree'\\n    and t.typname = 'ltree'\\n    and n.nspname not in ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema')\\n  group by n.nspname, c.relname, ic.relname\\n) s\\nwhere (xpath(\\n         '/row/cnt/text()',\\n         query_to_xml(\\n           format('select count(*) as cnt from %I.%I where %s(%s)',\\n                  s.schema_name,\\n                  s.table_name,\\n                  case when s.pred is not null then '(' || s.pred || ') and ' else '' end,\\n                  s.keys_cond),\\n           false,\\n           true,\\n           ''\\n         )\\n       ))[1]::text::bigint > 0\\norder by 1;\\n```\\n\\n### 2. pgcrypto legacy ciphers (CVE-2026-14663)\\n\\nIf you call `pgp_sym_encrypt`/`pgp_pub_encrypt` (or their `_bytea` variants) with `cipher-algo=bf`, `cipher-algo=blowfish`, or `cipher-algo=cast5`, that data was effectively stored **unencrypted** — decryption succeeds even with the wrong key.\\nThe default cipher (AES) and `3des` are not affected.\\nIf you never passed a `cipher-algo` option, no action is needed.\\n\\nTo find affected rows, scan each stored value with a deliberately wrong passphrase: properly encrypted values raise an error, while affected values decrypt successfully even with the wrong key.\\nRun the helper and the scan in the same session (`pg_temp` functions are session-scoped):\\n\\n```sql\\ncreate function pg_temp.affected_by_cve_2026_14663(msg bytea)\\nreturns boolean\\nlanguage plpgsql as $$\\nbegin\\n  perform pgp_sym_decrypt_bytea(msg, 'deliberately-wrong-key');\\n  return true;\\nexception when others then\\n  return false;\\nend $$;\\n\\nselect <id_column>\\nfrom <your_table>\\nwhere <your_encrypted_column> is not null\\n  and pg_temp.affected_by_cve_2026_14663(<your_encrypted_column>);\\n```\\n\\nAny rows returned hold affected values.\\nThe scan covers symmetric (`pgp_sym_*`) messages.\\nThe wrong-key probe does not apply to public-key (`pgp_pub_*`) messages.\\nIf `pgp_pub_encrypt` was used with an affected `cipher-algo`, treat those values as affected and re-encrypt them the same way using `pgp_pub_decrypt` and `pgp_pub_encrypt` with the key pair.\\n\\n### 3. btree_gist indexes on float columns\\n\\nIndexes built under the previous version can return wrong results for rows containing `NaN` until reindexed.\\nFind `btree_gist` indexes on float columns:\\n\\n```sql\\nselect distinct\\n  n.nspname as schema_name,\\n  cls.relname as table_name,\\n  ic.relname as index_name\\nfrom pg_index idx\\n  join pg_class ic on idx.indexrelid = ic.oid\\n  join pg_am am on ic.relam = am.oid\\n  join pg_class cls on idx.indrelid = cls.oid\\n  join pg_namespace n on ic.relnamespace = n.oid\\n  join lateral unnest(idx.indclass::oid[]) with ordinality as k(opclass, pos) on true\\n  join pg_opclass oc on oc.oid = k.opclass\\n  join pg_type ty on ty.oid = oc.opcintype\\nwhere\\n  am.amname = 'gist'\\n  and k.pos <= idx.indnkeyatts\\n  and ty.typname in ('float4', 'float8');\\n```\\n\\nYou are affected only if indexes are returned and those columns may contain `NaN` values.\\n\\n### 4. Custom operators (CVE-2026-2004)\\n\\nOnly superusers may now attach a non-built-in selectivity estimator to an operator.\\nExisting operators keep working.\\nOnly re-creation (dump/restore, branching, major-version upgrade) fails.\\n\\nOperators installed by extensions (PostGIS, intarray, etc.) are not affected.\\nCheck for affected operators:\\n\\n```sql\\nselect\\n  n.nspname as schema, o.oprname as operator,\\n  o.oprrest::regproc as restrict_estimator,\\n  o.oprjoin::regproc as join_estimator\\nfrom pg_operator o\\njoin pg_namespace n on o.oprnamespace = n.oid\\nwhere n.nspname not in ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema')\\n  and ((o.oprrest <> 0 and o.oprrest::oid >= 10000)\\n    or (o.oprjoin <> 0 and o.oprjoin::oid >= 10000))\\n  and not exists (\\n    select 1 from pg_depend d\\n    where d.classid = 'pg_operator'::regclass and d.objid = o.oid and d.deptype = 'e'\\n  );\\n```\\n\\n## What happens if you take no action\\n\\n- **ltree / btree_gist:** affected index searches may silently return wrong or incomplete results - no error is raised.\\n- **pgcrypto:** decryption of affected messages fails by default after the upgrade (recoverable with the `ignore-cipher-failure=1` decrypt option).\\n  The underlying data remains effectively unencrypted at rest until re-encrypted.\\n- **Custom operators:** a future dump/restore, branch, or major-version upgrade fails to recreate the operator.\\n\\n## Migration steps\\n\\n1. Run the detection queries above for each database.\\n2. After upgrading, reindex each affected ltree/btree_gist index using its schema-qualified name — `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY <schema_name>.<index_name>;` runs online with no downtime, but cannot run inside a transaction block.\\n3. For pgcrypto: re-encrypt affected values with a modern cipher (for example `cipher-algo=aes256`), before the upgrade or after it using `ignore-cipher-failure=1`, and consider rotating secrets stored this way.\\n4. For custom operators: recreate without the `RESTRICT`/`JOIN` clause (or with a built-in estimator), or contact support and we'll assist.\\n\\n## Rollout timeline\\n\\n| Date       | Milestone                                            | User action                       |\\n| ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |\\n| 2026-09-25 | Release announce (this entry)                        | Run detection queries             |\\n| 2026-09-28 | New projects created on 15.19 / 17.11                | —                                 |\\n| 2026-09-28 | [Upgrade](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/platform/upgrading) available in dashboard for existing projects | Upgrade, then reindex if affected |\\n\\r\\n\"}"}], "internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough": {"turn_id": "01a1db92-c572-7ff2-8efd-dbb7dc570992", "create_time": 1794685417.1441803}}, "metadata": {"history_sequence": 438, "sampled_through_sequence": 435, "client_authored": false, "fallback_token_limit_override": 12000}}

Then look up the relevant topic using the documentation access methods below.\r\n\r\n**2. Verify your work.**\r\nAfter implementing any fix, run a test query to confirm the change works. A fix without verification is incomplete.\r\n\r\n**3. Recover from errors, don't loop.**\r\nIf an approach fails after 2-3 attempts, stop and reconsider. Try a different method, check documentation, inspect the error more carefully, and review relevant logs when available. Supabase issues are not always solved by retrying the same command, and the answer is not always in the logs, but logs are often worth checking before proceeding.\r\n\r\n**4. Exposing tables to the Data API:** Depending on the user's [Data API settings](https://supabase.com/dashboard/project/<ref>/integrations/data_api/settings), newly created tables may not be automatically exposed via the Data (REST) API. If this is the case, `anon` and `authenticated` roles will need to be explicitly granted access.\r\n\r\n> Note that this is separate from RLS, which controls which _rows_ are visible once a table is accessible, not whether the table is accessible at all.\r\n\r\nWhen a user reports a SQL-created table is unexpectedly inaccessible, check their Data API settings and whether the roles have been granted access via explicit `GRANT` SQL. When granting public (`anon`/`authenticated`) access, always enable RLS too. See [Exposing a Table to the Data API](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/api/securing-your-api.md) for the full setup workflow.\r\n\r\n**5. RLS in exposed schemas.**\r\nEnable RLS on every table in any exposed schema, which includes `public` by default. This is critical in Supabase because tables in exposed schemas can be reachable through the Data API when the `anon`/`authenticated` roles have access (see [Exposing a Table to the Data API](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/api/securing-your-api.md)). For private schemas, prefer RLS as defense in depth. After enabling RLS, create policies that match the actual access model rather than defaulting every table to the same `auth.uid()` pattern.\r\n\r\n**6. Security checklist.**\r\nWhen working on any Supabase task that touches auth, RLS, views, storage, or user data, run through this checklist. These are Supabase-specific security traps that silently create vulnerabilities:\r\n\r\n- **Auth and session security**\r\n  - **Never use `user_metadata` claims in JWT-based authorization decisions.** In Supabase, `raw_user_meta_data` is user-editable and can appear in `auth.jwt()`, so it is unsafe for RLS policies or any other authorization logic. Store authorization data in `raw_app_meta_data` / `app_metadata` instead.\r\n  - **Deleting a user does not invalidate existing access tokens.** Sign out or revoke sessions first, keep JWT expiry short for sensitive apps, and for strict guarantees validate `session_id` against `auth.sessions` on sensitive operations.\r\n  - **If you use `app_metadata` or `auth.jwt()` for authorization, remember JWT claims are not always fresh until the user's token is refreshed.**\r\n\r\n- **API key and client exposure**\r\n  - **Never expose the `service_role` or secret key in public clients.** Prefer publishable keys for frontend code. Legacy `anon` keys are only for compatibility. In Next.js, any `NEXT_PUBLIC_` env var is sent to the browser.\r\n  - **Use scoped personal access tokens for the Management API, CLI, and MCP server.** A classic personal access token carries the user's full account access, on every organization and project. For scripts, CI, and agents, have the user create a scoped token limited to the organizations, projects, and permissions the task needs. The [personal access tokens guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/platform/personal-access-tokens.md) lists the permission each Management API endpoint and MCP tool requires. Look permissions up there rather than guessing.\r\n\r\n- **RLS, views, and privileged database code**\r\n  - **Views bypass RLS by default.** In Postgres 15 and above, use `CREATE VIEW ... WITH (security_invoker = true)`. In older versions of Postgres, protect your views by revoking access from the `anon` and `authenticated` roles, or by putting them in an unexposed schema.\r\n  - **UPDATE requires a SELECT policy.** In Postgres RLS, an UPDATE needs to first SELECT the row. Without a SELECT policy, updates silently return 0 rows â€” no error, just no change.\r\n  - **`auth.role()` is deprecated â€” use the `TO` clause instead.** Supabase has deprecated `auth.role()` in favour of specifying the target role directly on the policy with `TO authenticated` or `TO anon`. Beyond deprecation, `auth.role() = 'authenticated'` breaks silently when anonymous sign-ins are enabled, because anonymous users carry the `authenticated` Postgres role and pass the check regardless of whether the user is genuinely signed in.\r\n    ```sql\r\n    -- Deprecated (do not use)\r\n    create policy \"example\" on table_name for select\r\n    using ( auth.role() = 'authenticated' );\r\n    ```\r\n  - **`TO authenticated` alone is authentication without authorization (BOLA / IDOR).** Using `TO authenticated` only checks the role â€” it does not restrict which rows a user can access. The correct pattern combines `TO authenticated` with an ownership predicate in `USING`:\r\n    ```sql\r\n    create policy \"example\" on table_name for select\r\n    to authenticated\r\n    using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );\r\n    ```\r\n  - **UPDATE policies require both `USING` and `WITH CHECK`.** Without `WITH CHECK`, a user can reassign a row's `user_id` to another user:\r\n    ```sql\r\n    create policy \"example\" on table_name for update\r\n    to authenticated\r\n    using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id )\r\n    with check ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );\r\n    ```\r\n  - **`SECURITY DEFINER` functions bypass RLS.** A `SECURITY DEFINER` function runs with its creator's privileges â€” typically a role with `bypassrls` (e.g., `postgres`). Never add `SECURITY DEFINER` to resolve a permission error; it silently removes access control without fixing the underlying cause. Prefer `SECURITY INVOKER`.\r\n  - **`SECURITY DEFINER` functions in `public` are callable by all roles.** Postgres grants `EXECUTE` to `PUBLIC` by default for every new function, so any `SECURITY DEFINER` function in `public` is a public API endpoint callable by `anon` and `authenticated` (which inherit from `PUBLIC`) without any additional grant. When `SECURITY DEFINER` is genuinely needed (e.g., bypassing RLS on an internal lookup table), keep the function in a non-exposed schema, always include an `auth.uid()` check in the function body, and run `supabase db advisors` after making changes.\r\n\r\n- **Storage access control**\r\n  - **Storage upsert requires INSERT + SELECT + UPDATE.** Granting only INSERT allows new uploads but file replacement (upsert) silently fails. You need all three.\r\n\r\n- **Dependency and supply-chain security**\r\n  - **Always pin package versions and commit lockfiles** when installing Supabase packages (`supabase-js`, `@supabase/ssr`, `supabase-py`, etc.). See the [npm security guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/security/npm-security.md) for the full checklist.\r\n\r\nFor any security concern not covered above, fetch the Supabase product security index: `https://supabase.com/docs/guides/security/product-security.md`\r\n\r\n## Supabase CLI\r\n\r\nAlways discover commands via `--help` â€” never guess. The CLI structure changes between versions.\r\n\r\n```bash\r\nsupabase --help                    # All top-level commands\r\nsupabase <group> --help            # Subcommands (e.g., supabase db --help)\r\nsupabase <group> <command> --help  # Flags for a specific command\r\n```\r\n\r\n**Supabase CLI Known gotchas:**\r\n\r\n- `supabase db query` requires **CLI v2.79.0+** â†’ use MCP `execute_sql` or `psql` as fallback\r\n- `supabase db advisors` requires **CLI v2.81.3+** â†’ use MCP `get_advisors` as fallback\r\n- The browser flow of `supabase login` creates a classic token with full account access. In CI, set `SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN` to a scoped personal access token instead. It takes precedence over any saved login. Commands that connect with the database password (`--password` or `SUPABASE_DB_PASSWORD`, for example `supabase db push`) aren't limited by the token's permissions.\r\n- In imperative migration projects, create new hand-authored migration files with `supabase migration new <name>` first. Never invent a migration filename or rely on memory for the expected format. Declarative schema projects generate migrations from `supabase/schemas/`; see \"Making and Committing Schema Changes\" below.\r\n\r\n**Version check and upgrade:** Run `supabase --version` to check. For CLI changelogs and version-specific features, consult the [CLI documentation](https://supabase.com/docs/reference/cli/introduction) or [GitHub releases](https://github.com/supabase/cli/releases).\r\n\r\n## Supabase MCP Server\r\n\r\nFor setup instructions, server URL, and configuration, see the [MCP setup guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/getting-started/mcp).\r\n\r\n**Troubleshooting connection issues** â€” follow these steps in order:\r\n\r\n1. **Check if the server is reachable:**\r\n   `curl -so /dev/null -w \"%{http_code}\" https://mcp.supabase.com/mcp`\r\n   A `401` is expected (no token) and means the server is up. Timeout or \"connection refused\" means it may be down.\r\n\r\n2. **Check `.mcp.json` configuration:**\r\n   Verify the project root has a valid `.mcp.json` with the correct server URL. If missing, create one pointing to `https://mcp.supabase.com/mcp`.\r\n\r\n3. **Authenticate the MCP server:**\r\n   If the server is reachable and `.mcp.json` is correct but tools aren't visible, the user needs to authenticate. The Supabase MCP server uses OAuth 2.1 â€” tell the user to trigger the auth flow in their agent, complete it in the browser, and reload the session.\r\n   In CI or other environments where the browser flow can't run, pass a scoped personal access token in the `Authorization: Bearer` header instead.\r\n\r\n4. **Check scoped token permissions:**\r\n   If a tool fails with \"You do not have permission to perform this action\" while using a scoped personal access token, the token lacks that tool's permission or the project is outside the token's scope. Check the tool's required permission in the [personal access tokens guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/platform/personal-access-tokens.md#mcp-tools).\r\n\r\n## Supabase Documentation\r\n\r\nBefore implementing any Supabase feature, find the relevant documentation. Use these methods in priority order:\r\n\r\n1. **MCP `search_docs` tool** (preferred â€” returns relevant snippets directly)\r\n2. **Fetch docs pages as markdown** â€” any docs page can be fetched by appending `.md` to the URL path.\r\n3. **Web search** for Supabase-specific topics when you don't know which page to look at.\r\n\r\n## Making and Committing Schema Changes\r\n\r\nFirst decide which schema workflow the project uses.\r\n\r\n### Option A: Declarative schemas\r\n\r\nUse this when `supabase/schemas/` exists or `config.toml` sets `schema_paths`. Edit the desired schema state in those files, then generate and review the migration. Do not start by hand-writing a migration. See the [Declarative database schemas guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/local-development/declarative-database-schemas).\r\n\r\n### Option B: Imperative migrations\r\n\r\nUse this when the project does not use declarative schemas.\r\n\r\n**To make schema changes, use `execute_sql` (MCP) or `supabase db query` (CLI).** These run SQL directly on the database without creating migration history entries, so you can iterate freely and generate a clean migration when ready.\r\n\r\nDo NOT use `apply_migration` to change a local database schema â€” it writes a migration history entry on every call, which means you can't iterate, and `supabase db diff` / `supabase db pull` will produce empty or conflicting diffs. If you use it, you'll be stuck with whatever SQL you passed on the first try.\r\n\r\n**When ready to commit** your changes to a migration file:\r\n\r\n1. **Run advisors** â†’ `supabase db advisors` (CLI v2.81.3+) or MCP `get_advisors`. Fix any issues.\r\n2. **Review the Security Checklist above** if your changes involve views, functions, triggers, or storage.\r\n3. **Generate the migration** â†’ `supabase db pull <descriptive-name> --local --yes`\r\n4. **Verify** â†’ `supabase migration list --local`\r\n\r\n## Debugging\r\n\r\nWhen you get an error on a Supabase-related request, for example an error code from the Supabase REST API, Postgres database, or PostgREST, an empty result, getting blocked by RLS unexpectedly, or an error from a Supabase service like Auth, Realtime, Edge Functions, or Storage, you **must** fetch Supabase's [Monitoring and Debugging](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/monitoring-and-debugging.md) documentation before diagnosing or proposing a fix, rather than working from memory. Security checklist.**\\r\\nWhen working on any Supabase task that touches auth, RLS, views, storage, or user data, run through this checklist. These are Supabase-specific security traps that silently create vulnerabilities:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Auth and session security**\\r\\n  - **Never use `user_metadata` claims in JWT-based authorization decisions.** In Supabase, `raw_user_meta_data` is user-editable and can appear in `auth.jwt()`, so it is unsafe for RLS policies or any other authorization logic. Store authorization data in `raw_app_meta_data` / `app_metadata` instead.\\r\\n  - **Deleting a user does not invalidate existing access tokens.** Sign out or revoke sessions first, keep JWT expiry short for sensitive apps, and for strict guarantees validate `session_id` against `auth.sessions` on sensitive operations.\\r\\n  - **If you use `app_metadata` or `auth.jwt()` for authorization, remember JWT claims are not always fresh until the user's token is refreshed.**\\r\\n\\r\\n- **API key and client exposure**\\r\\n  - **Never expose the `service_role` or secret key in public clients.** Prefer publishable keys for frontend code. Legacy `anon` keys are only for compatibility. In Next.js, any `NEXT_PUBLIC_` env var is sent to the browser.\\r\\n  - **Use scoped personal access tokens for the Management API, CLI, and MCP server.** A classic personal access token carries the user's full account access, on every organization and project. For scripts, CI, and agents, have the user create a scoped token limited to the organizations, projects, and permissions the task needs. The [personal access tokens guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/platform/personal-access-tokens.md) lists the permission each Management API endpoint and MCP tool requires. Look permissions up there rather than guessing.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **RLS, views, and privileged database code**\\r\\n  - **Views bypass RLS by default.** In Postgres 15 and above, use `CREATE VIEW ... WITH (security_invoker = true)`. In older versions of Postgres, protect your views by revoking access from the `anon` and `authenticated` roles, or by putting them in an unexposed schema.\\r\\n  - **UPDATE requires a SELECT policy.** In Postgres RLS, an UPDATE needs to first SELECT the row. Without a SELECT policy, updates silently return 0 rows â€” no error, just no change.\\r\\n  - **`auth.role()` is deprecated â€” use the `TO` clause instead.** Supabase has deprecated `auth.role()` in favour of specifying the target role directly on the policy with `TO authenticated` or `TO anon`. Beyond deprecation, `auth.role() = 'authenticated'` breaks silently when anonymous sign-ins are enabled, because anonymous users carry the `authenticated` Postgres role and pass the check regardless of whether the user is genuinely signed in.\\r\\n    ```sql\\r\\n    -- Deprecated (do not use)\\r\\n    create policy \\\"example\\\" on table_name for select\\r\\n    using ( auth.role() = 'authenticated' );\\r\\n    ```\\r\\n  - **`TO authenticated` alone is authentication without authorization (BOLA / IDOR).** Using `TO authenticated` only checks the role â€” it does not restrict which rows a user can access. The correct pattern combines `TO authenticated` with an ownership predicate in `USING`:\\r\\n    ```sql\\r\\n    create policy \\\"example\\\" on table_name for select\\r\\n    to authenticated\\r\\n    using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );\\r\\n    ```\\r\\n  - **UPDATE policies require both `USING` and `WITH CHECK`.** Without `WITH CHECK`, a user can reassign a row's `user_id` to another user:\\r\\n    ```sql\\r\\n    create policy \\\"example\\\" on table_name for update\\r\\n    to authenticated\\r\\n    using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id )\\r\\n    with check ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );\\r\\n    ```\\r\\n  - **`SECURITY DEFINER` functions bypass RLS.** A `SECURITY DEFINER` function runs with its creator's privileges â€” typically a role with `bypassrls` (e.g., `postgres`). Never add `SECURITY DEFINER` to resolve a permission error; it silently removes access control without fixing the underlying cause. Prefer `SECURITY INVOKER`.\\r\\n  - **`SECURITY DEFINER` functions in `public` are callable by all roles.** Postgres grants `EXECUTE` to `PUBLIC` by default for every new function, so any `SECURITY DEFINER` function in `public` is a public API endpoint callable by `anon` and `authenticated` (which inherit from `PUBLIC`) without any additional grant. When `SECURITY DEFINER` is genuinely needed (e.g., bypassing RLS on an internal lookup table), keep the function in a non-exposed schema, always include an `auth.uid()` check in the function body, and run `supabase db advisors` after making changes.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Storage access control**\\r\\n  - **Storage upsert requires INSERT + SELECT + UPDATE.** Granting only INSERT allows new uploads but file replacement (upsert) silently fails. You need all three.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Dependency and supply-chain security**\\r\\n  - **Always pin package versions and commit lockfiles** when installing Supabase packages (`supabase-js`, `@supabase/ssr`, `supabase-py`, etc.). background processes and utilities. Helps diagnose and detect performance and operational issues.\\n\\n\\n### `log_autovacuum_min_duration`\\n\\n`update` and `delete` commands leave behind obsolete row versions to support rollbacks and concurrent queries. A background process called the [Autovacuum](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/routine-vacuuming.html#AUTOVACUUM) permanently removes the rows in batch jobs at a later point. The setting logs Autovacuum when they run longer than the limit.\\n\\n**Useful for:**\\n\\n*   Monitoring vacuum activity\\n*   Identifying resource strain, such as [IO usage](/docs/guides/platform/manage-your-usage/disk-iops), caused by vacuums\\n\\n**Example logs:**\\n\\n```sh\\n# records tables vacuumed\\nautomatic vacuum of table \\\"postgres.public.vac_test\\\": index scans: 0\\nautomatic analyze of table \\\"postgres.public.vac_test\\\"\\n```\\n\\n<Accordion type=\\\"default\\\" chevronAlign=\\\"right\\\" justified size=\\\"medium\\\" className=\\\"text-foreground-light mt-8 mb-6\\\">\\n  <AccordionItem header=\\\"Configuration examples\\\" id=\\\"item-1\\\">\\n    <NamedCodeBlock name=\\\"API\\\">\\n      ```sh name=API\\n      curl https://api.supabase.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_REF/config/database/postgres \\\\\\n        --request PUT \\\\\\n        --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \\\\\\n        --header 'Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN' \\\\\\n        --data '{\\n        \\\"log_autovacuum_min_duration\\\": \\\"0ms\\\"\\n      }'\\n      ```\\n    </NamedCodeBlock>\\n\\n    <NamedCodeBlock name=\\\"CLI\\\">\\n      ```sh name=CLI\\n      supabase --experimental \\\\\\n      postgres-config update --config log_autovacuum_min_duration=10ms \\\\\\n      --project-ref <project-ref>\\n      ```\\n    </NamedCodeBlock>\\n  </AccordionItem>\\n</Accordion>\\n\\n\\n### `log_checkpoints`\\n\\nCheckpoints are background operations that write modified data from memory to disk. It enables Postgres to discard [WAL files](/docs/guides/database/replication#write-ahead-log-wal) that otherwise must be retained for data recovery and replication.\\n\\nThe setting records automatic checkpoint events.\\n\\n**Useful for:**\\n\\n*   Measuring checkpoint write volume\\n*   Identifying excessive checkpoint-related disk activity\\n*   Detecting read-replica issues\\n*   Deciding whether checkpoint settings should be adjusted\\n\\n**Example logs:**\\n\\n```sh\\n# Monitoring checkpointer activity\\ncheckpoint starting: time\\ncheckpoint complete: wrote 405563 buffers (6.4%); 0 WAL file(s) added, 0 removed, 465 recycled; write=269.656 s, sync=3.570 s, total=274.133 s; sync files=2393, longest=0.375 s, average=0.002 s; distance=6635965 kB, estimate=7953512 kB\\n```\\n\\n```sh\\n# Monitoring replay activity from read replicas\\nrestartpoint starting: time\\nrecovery restart point at 0/B837D6F0\\nrestartpoint complete: wrote 266 buffers (0.4%); For more information on lock management, reference [postgreslocksexplained.com](https://postgreslocksexplained.com/locks/concept).\\n\\n**Useful for:**\\n\\n*   Identifying queries that are blocked by locks\\n*   Identifying which queries are blocking\\n*   Measuring how long queries remain blocked\\n\\n**Example logs:**\\n\\n```sh\\n# records when a process is waiting on a lock for 1+s\\nprocess 1017208 still waiting for \\\"lock_type\\\" on relation 75874 of database 5 after 1001.872 ms\\n```\\n\\n```sh\\n# records when a process is finally able to claim its lock\\nprocess 1007982 acquired \\\"lock_type\\\" on transaction 445264 after 2000.880 ms\\n```\\n\\n<Accordion type=\\\"default\\\" chevronAlign=\\\"right\\\" justified size=\\\"medium\\\" className=\\\"text-foreground-light mt-8 mb-6\\\">\\n  <AccordionItem header=\\\"Configuration examples\\\" id=\\\"item-1\\\">\\n    <NamedCodeBlock name=\\\"API\\\">\\n      ```sh name=API\\n      curl https://api.supabase.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_REF/config/database/postgres \\\\\\n        --request PUT \\\\\\n        --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \\\\\\n        --header 'Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN' \\\\\\n        --data '{\\n        \\\"log_lock_waits\\\": false\\n      }'\\n      ```\\n    </NamedCodeBlock>\\n\\n    <NamedCodeBlock name=\\\"CLI\\\">\\n      ```sh name=CLI\\n      supabase --experimental \\\\\\n      postgres-config update --config log_lock_waits=true \\\\\\n      --project-ref <project-ref>\\n      ```\\n    </NamedCodeBlock>\\n\\n    <NamedCodeBlock name=\\\"SQL\\\">\\n      ```sql name=SQL\\n      alter role \\\"postgres\\\" set log_lock_waits to true;\\n      ```\\n    </NamedCodeBlock>\\n  </AccordionItem>\\n</Accordion>\\n\\n\\n### `log_recovery_conflict_waits`\\n\\nIf a read-replica is acting on data that is being modified/discarded by the primary, then it may wait to determine if the data should be available or not before responding. The setting `log_recovery_conflict_waits` determines if the replica should report waits that last more than `1s`.\\n\\n**Useful for:**\\n\\n*   Detecting operations that interfere with replica queries\\n*   Detecting operations that may cause replication lag\\n\\n**Example log:**\\n\\n```sh\\nrecovery still waiting after 1000.156 ms: recovery conflict on lock\\n```\\n\\n<Accordion type=\\\"default\\\" chevronAlign=\\\"right\\\" justified size=\\\"medium\\\" className=\\\"text-foreground-light mt-8 mb-6\\\">\\n  <AccordionItem header=\\\"Configuration examples\\\" id=\\\"item-1\\\">\\n    <NamedCodeBlock name=\\\"API\\\">\\n      ```sh name=API\\n      curl https://api.supabase.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_REF/config/database/postgres \\\\\\n        --request PUT \\\\\\n        --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \\\\\\n        --header 'Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN' \\\\\\n        --data '{\\n        \\\"log_recovery_conflict_waits\\\": true\\n      }'\\n      ```\\n    </NamedCodeBlock>\\n\\n    <NamedCodeBlock name=\\\"CLI\\\">\\n      ```sh name=CLI\\n      supabase --experimental \\\\\\n      postgres-config update --config log_recovery_conflict_waits=true \\\\\\n      --project-ref <project-ref>\\n      ```\\n    </NamedCodeBlock>\\n  </AccordionItem>\\n</Accordion>\\n\\n\\n### `log_startup_progress_interval`\\n\\nWhen a server is recovering from a crash, it has to go through several checks before it becomes operational again. When these operations exceed the memory limits primarily managed by the [work\\\\_mem](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html#GUC-WORK-MEM) and [hash\\\\_mem\\\\_multiplier](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html#GUC-HASH-MEM-MULTIPLIER) settings, Postgres uses temporary files on disk to complete them.\\n\\nWhen temp files larger than the `log_temp_files` limit are created, Postgres logs the event, helping identify queries that can benefit from memory tuning.\\n\\n**Useful for:**\\n\\n*   Determining when the You can use these APIs to fetch and insert data from the frontend, as long as you have [RLS](/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security) enabled.\\n\\n*   [REST](/docs/guides/api)\\n*   [GraphQL](/docs/guides/graphql/api)\\n\\nFor convenience, you can also use the [Supabase client libraries](/docs/reference), which wrap the Data APIs with a developer-friendly interface and automatically handle authentication:\\n\\n*   [JavaScript](/docs/reference/javascript)\\n*   [Flutter](/docs/reference/dart)\\n*   [Swift](/docs/reference/swift)\\n*   [Python](/docs/reference/python)\\n*   [C#](/docs/reference/csharp)\\n*   [Kotlin](/docs/reference/kotlin)\\n\\n\\n## Direct connection\\n\\nThe direct connection string connects directly to your Postgres instance. It is ideal for persistent servers, such as virtual machines (VMs) and long-lasting containers. Examples include AWS EC2 machines, Fly.io VMs, and DigitalOcean Droplets.\\n\\n<Admonition type=\\\"caution\\\">\\n  Direct connections are on IPv6, or on IPv4 if the project has the [IPv4 add-on](/docs/guides/platform/ipv4-address). If your network is IPv4-only and you don't have the add-on, use [pooler session mode](#pooler-session-mode) instead.\\n</Admonition>\\n\\nThe connection string looks like this:\\n\\n```\\npostgresql://postgres:[YOUR-PASSWORD]@db.abcdefghijklmnopqrst.supabase.co:5432/postgres\\n```\\n\\nGet your project's direct connection string from your project dashboard by clicking [Connect](/dashboard/project/_?showConnect=true).\\n\\n\\n## Poolers\\n\\nSupabase offers two poolers. The **Shared Pooler** ([Supavisor](https://github.com/supabase/supavisor)) is multi-tenant, available on every project, and IPv4-only. The **Dedicated Pooler** ([PgBouncer](https://www.pgbouncer.org/)) is available on paid plans and co-located with your Postgres instance; like the direct connection, it is on IPv6, or on IPv4 if the project has the [IPv4 add-on](/docs/guides/platform/ipv4-address).\\n\\n\\n### Pooler session mode\\n\\nThe session mode connection string connects to your Postgres instance via the Shared Pooler (Supavisor). This is only recommended as an alternative to a Direct Connection when connecting from an IPv4-only network.\\n\\nThe connection string looks like this:\\n\\n```\\npostgres://postgres.apbkobhfnmcqqzqeeqss:[YOUR-PASSWORD]@aws-[REGION].pooler.supabase.com:5432/postgres\\n```\\n\\nGet your project's Session pooler connection string from your project dashboard by clicking [Connect](/dashboard/project/_?showConnect=true\\\\&method=session).\\n\\n\\n### Pooler transaction mode\\n\\nThe transaction mode connection string connects to your Postgres instance via the Shared Pooler (Supavisor) in transaction-pooling mode. This is ideal for serverless or edge functions, which require many transient connections.\\n\\n<Admonition type=\\\"caution\\\">\\n  Transaction mode does not support [prepared statements](https://postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-prepare.html). To avoid errors, [turn off prepared statements](https://github.com/orgs/supabase/discussions/28239) for your connection library.\\n</Admonition>\\n\\nThe connection string looks like this:\\n\\n```\\npostgres://postgres.apbkobhfnmcqqzqeeqss:[YOUR-PASSWORD]@aws-[REGION].pooler.supabase.com:6543/postgres\\n```\\n\\nGet your project's Transaction pooler connection string from your project dashboard by clicking [Connect](/dashboard/project/_?showConnect=true\\\\&method=transaction).\\n\\n\\n## Dedicated pooler\\n\\nFor paying customers, we provision a Dedicated Pooler ([PgBouncer](https://www.pgbouncer.org/)) that's co-located with your Postgres database. The Dedicated Pooler runs in transaction mode only - for session mode, use the [Shared Pooler](#pooler-session-mode). It is reachable over IPv6, or over IPv4 if the project has the [IPv4 add-on](/docs/guides/platform/ipv4-address).\\n\\nThe connection string looks like this:\\n\\n```\\npostgres://postgres:[YOUR-PASSWORD]@db.abcdefghijklmnopqrst.supabase.co:6543/postgres\\n```\\n\\nThe Dedicated Pooler ensures best performance and latency, while using up more of your project's compute resources. If your network supports IPv6 or you have the IPv4 add-on, we encourage you to use the Dedicated Pooler over the Shared Pooler.\\n\\nGet your project's Dedicated pooler connection string from your project dashboard by clicking [Connect](/dashboard/project/_?showConnect=true\\\\&method=transaction).\\n\\n\\n## More about connection pooling\\n\\nConnection pooling improves database performance by reusing existing connections between queries. This reduces the overhead of establishing connections and improves scalability.\\n\\nYou can use an application-side pooler or a server-side pooler (Supabase automatically provides one called Supavisor), depending on whether your backend is persistent or serverless.\\n\\n\\n### Application-side poolers\\n\\nApplication-side poolers are built into connection libraries and API servers, such as Prisma, SQLAlchemy, and PostgREST. They maintain several active connections with Postgres or a server-side pooler, reducing the overhead of establishing connections between queries. When deploying to static architecture, such as long-standing containers or VMs, application-side poolers are satisfactory on their own.\\n\\n\\n### Server-side poolers\\n\\nPostgres connections are like a WebSocket. Once established, they are preserved until the client (application server) disconnects. A server might only make a single 10 ms query, but needlessly reserve its database connection for seconds or longer.\\n\\nServer-side poolers, such as Supabase's [Supavisor](https://github.com/supabase/supavisor) in transaction mode, sit between clients and the database and can be thought of as load balancers for Postgres connections.\\n\\n<Image\\n  alt=\\\"New migration files trigger migrations on the preview instance.\\\"\\n  src={{\\n    dark: '/docs/img/guides/database/connecting-to-postgres/how-connection-pooling-works.png',\\n    light:\\n      '/docs/img/guides/database/connecting-to-postgres/how-connection-pooling-works--light.png',\\n  }}\\n  width={1851}\\n  height={907}\\n  caption=\\\"Connecting to the database directly vs using a Connection Pooler\\\"\\n/>\\n\\nThey maintain hot connections with the database and intelligently share them with clients only when needed, maximizing the amount of queries a single connection can service. They're best used to manage queries from auto-scaling systems, such as edge and serverless functions.\\n\\n\\n## Connecting with SSL\\n\\nYou should connect to your database using SSL wherever possible, to prevent snooping and man-in-the-middle attacks.\\n\\nYou can obtain your connection info and Server root certificate from your application's dashboard:\\n\\n![Connection Info and Certificate.](/docs/img/database/database-settings-ssl.png)\\n\\n\\n## Resources\\n\\n*   [Connection management](/docs/guides/database/connection-management)\\n*   [Connecting with psql](/docs/guides/database/psql)\\n*   [Importing data into Supabase](/docs/guides/database/import-data)\\n\\n\\n## Troubleshooting and Postgres connection string FAQs\\n\\nBelow are answers to common challenges and queries.\\n\\n\\n### What is a “connection refused” error?\\n\\nA “Connection refused” error typically means your database isn’t reachable. Ensure your Supabase project is running, confirm your database’s connection string, check firewall settings, and validate network permissions.\\n\\n\\n### What is the “FATAL: Password authentication failed” error?\\n\\nThis error occurs when your credentials are incorrect. Double-check your username and password from the Supabase dashboard. If the problem persists, reset your database password from the project settings.\\n\\n\\n### How do you connect using IPv4?\\n\\nYou have two options. The Shared Pooler (Supavisor) is IPv4-only on every project tier - use it in either session or transaction mode. Alternatively, add the [IPv4 add-on](/docs/guides/platform/ipv4-address) to your project, which makes the direct connection and Dedicated Pooler reachable over IPv4 instead of IPv6.\\n\\n\\n### Where is the Postgres connection string in Supabase?\\n\\nYour connection string is located in the Supabase Dashboard. Click the [Connect](/dashboard/project/_?showConnect=true) button at the top of the page.\\n\\n\\n### Can you use Supavisor and PgBouncer together?\\n\\nYou can technically use both, but it’s not recommended unless you’re specifically trying to increase the total number of concurrent client connections. In most cases, it is better to choose either PgBouncer or Supavisor for pooled or transaction-based traffic. Direct connections remain the best choice for long-lived sessions, and, if IPv4 is required for those sessions, Supavisor session mode can be used as an alternative. Running both poolers simultaneously increases the risk of hitting your database’s maximum connection limit on smaller compute tiers.\\n\\n\\n### How does the default pool size work?\\n\\nSupavisor and PgBouncer work independently, but both reference the same pool size setting. For example, If you set the pool size to 30, Supavisor can open up to 30 server side connections to Postgres. These connections are shared between the session mode port (5432) and the transaction mode port (6543). Each mode can use up to 30 connections independently, or split them between both, but the total combined connections across both modes cannot exceed 30. PgBouncer can also open up to 30 connections under the same limit. If both poolers are active and reach their roles/modes limits at the same time, you could have as many as 60 backend connections hitting your database, in addition to any direct connections. You can adjust the pool size in [Database settings](/dashboard/project/_/database/settings) in the dashboard.\\n\\n\\n### What is the difference between client connections and backend connections?\\n\\nThere are two different limits to understand when working with poolers. The first is client connections, which refers to how many clients can connect to a pooler at the same time. This number is capped by your [compute tier’s “max pooler clients” limit](/docs/guides/platform/compute-and-disk#postgres-replication-slots-wal-senders-and-connections), and it applies independently to Supavisor and PgBouncer. The second is backend connections, which is the number of active connections a pooler opens to Postgres. This number is set by the pool size for that pooler.\\n\\n```\\nTotal backend load on Postgres =\\n Direct connections +\\n Supavisor backend connections (≤ supavisor_pool_size) +\\n PgBouncer backend connections (≤ pgbouncer_pool_size)\\n≤ Postgres max connections for your compute instance\\n```\\n\\n\\n### What is the max pooler clients limit?\\n\\nThe “max pooler clients” limit for your compute tier applies separately to Supavisor and PgBouncer. One pooler reaching its client limit does not affect the other. When a pooler reaches this limit, it stops accepting new client connections until existing ones are closed, but the other pooler remains unaffected. You can check your tier’s connection limits in the [compute and disk limits documentation](/docs/guides/platform/compute-and-disk#postgres-replication-slots-wal-senders-and-connections).\\n\\n\\n### Where can you see current connection usage?\\n\\nYou can track connection usage from the [Observability](/dashboard/project/_/observability/database) section in your project dashboard. There are three key reports:\\n\\n*   **Database Connections:** shows total active connections by role (this includes direct and pooled connections).\\n*   **Dedicated Pooler Client Connections:** shows the number of active client connections to PgBouncer.\\n*   **Shared Pooler (Supavisor) Client Connections:** shows the number of active client connections to Supavisor.\\n\\nKeep in mind that the Roles page is not real-time, it shows the connection count from the last refresh. If you need up-to-the-second data, set up Grafana or run the query against `pg_stat_activity` directly in SQL Editor. We have a few helpful queries for checking connections.\\n\\n```sql\\n-- Count connections by application and user name\\nselect\\n  count(usename),\\n  count(application_name),\\n  application_name,\\n  usename\\nfrom\\n  pg_stat_ssl\\n  join pg_stat_activity on pg_stat_ssl.pid = pg_stat_activity.pid\\ngroup by usename, application_name;\\n```\\n\\n```sql\\n-- View all connections\\n SELECT\\n   pg_stat_activity.pid,\\n   ssl AS ssl_connection,\\n   datname AS database,\\n   usename AS connected_role,\\n   application_name,\\n   client_addr,\\n   query,\\n   query_start,\\n   state,\\n   backend_start\\nFROM pg_stat_ssl\\nJOIN pg_stat_activity\\n ON pg_stat_ssl.pid = pg_stat_activity.pid;\\n```\\n\\n\\n### Why are there active connections when the app is idle?\\n\\nEven if your application isn’t making queries, some Supabase services keep persistent connections to your database. For example, Storage, PostgREST, and our health checker all maintain long-lived connections. You usually see a small baseline of active connections from these services.\\n\\n\\n### Why do connection strings have different ports?\\n\\nDifferent modes use different ports:\\n\\n*   Direct connection: `5432` (Postgres on your project instance)\\n*   Dedicated pooler, transaction mode: `6543` (PgBouncer on your project instance)\\n*   Shared pooler, transaction mode: `6543` (Supavisor, multi-tenant)\\n*   Shared pooler, session mode: `5432` (Supavisor, multi-tenant)\\n\\nThe port helps route the connection to the right pooler/mode.\\n\\n\\n### Does connection pooling affect latency?\\n\\nBecause the dedicated pooler is hosted on the same machine as your database, it connects with lower latency than the shared pooler, which is hosted on a separate server. Direct connections have no pooler overhead but require IPv6 unless you have the IPv4 add-on.\\n\\n\\n### How to choose the right connection method?\\n\\n**Direct connection:**\\n\\n*   Best for: persistent backend services\\n*   Use for migrations, pg\\\\_dump, backup and management tools\\n*   Network: reachable over IPv6, or over IPv4 if the project has the [IPv4 add-on](/docs/guides/platform/ipv4-address).\\n\\n**Shared pooler (Supavisor):**\\n\\n*   Best for: connections from IPv4 networks (IPv4-only on every tier)\\n    *   Supavisor session mode → persistent backend on IPv4 networks\\n    *   Supavisor transaction mode → serverless functions or short-lived tasks\\n*   Use for application runtime traffic (queries, writes)\\n\\n**Dedicated pooler (PgBouncer, paid tier):**\\n\\n*   Best for: high-performance apps that need dedicated resources\\n*   Use for application runtime traffic (queries, writes)\\n*   Transaction mode only - use the Shared Pooler if you need session mode\\n*   Network: reachable over IPv6, or over IPv4 if the project has the [IPv4 add-on](/docs/guides/platform/ipv4-address)\\n\\nSee the [connection method matrix](#how-to-connect-to-your-postgres-databases) at the top of this page for a quick reference, or follow the decision flow in the diagram below to choose the right option for your environment.\\n\\n<Image\\n  alt=\\\"Decision tree diagram showing when to connect directly to Postgres or use a connection pooler.\\\"\\n  src={{\\n    dark: '/docs/img/guides/database/connecting-to-postgres/connection-decision-tree.svg',\\n    light: '/docs/img/guides/database/connecting-to-postgres/connection-decision-tree-light.svg',\\n  }}\\n  caption=\\\"Choosing between direct Postgres connections and connection pooling\\\"\\n  width={291}\\n  height={150}\\n/>\\n\"}]}}}"}]}, "duration": {"secs": 1, "nanos": 70068700}}, "started_at_ms": 1794687351072, "completed_at_ms": 1794687352145}}

If this is the case, `anon` and `authenticated` roles will need to be explicitly granted access.\r\n\r\n> Note that this is separate from RLS, which controls which _rows_ are visible once a table is accessible, not whether the table is accessible at all.\r\n\r\nWhen a user reports a SQL-created table is unexpectedly inaccessible, check their Data API settings and whether the roles have been granted access via explicit `GRANT` SQL. See [Exposing a Table to the Data API](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/api/securing-your-api.md) for the full setup workflow.\r\n\r\n**5. RLS in exposed schemas.**\r\nEnable RLS on every table in any exposed schema, which includes `public` by default. This is critical in Supabase because tables in exposed schemas can be reachable through the Data API when the `anon`/`authenticated` roles have access (see [Exposing a Table to the Data API](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/api/securing-your-api.md)). For private schemas, prefer RLS as defense in depth. After enabling RLS, create policies that match the actual access model rather than defaulting every table to the same `auth.uid()` pattern.\r\n\r\n**6. Security checklist.**\r\nWhen working on any Supabase task that touches auth, RLS, views, storage, or user data, run through this checklist. These are Supabase-specific security traps that silently create vulnerabilities:\r\n\r\n- **Auth and session security**\r\n  - **Never use `user_metadata` claims in JWT-based authorization decisions.** In Supabase, `raw_user_meta_data` is user-editable and can appear in `auth.jwt()`, so it is unsafe for RLS policies or any other authorization logic. Store authorization data in `raw_app_meta_data` / `app_metadata` instead.\r\n  - **Deleting a user does not invalidate existing access tokens.** Sign out or revoke sessions first, keep JWT expiry short for sensitive apps, and for strict guarantees validate `session_id` against `auth.sessions` on sensitive operations.\r\n  - **If you use `app_metadata` or `auth.jwt()` for authorization, remember JWT claims are not always fresh until the user's token is refreshed.**\r\n\r\n- **API key and client exposure**\r\n  - **Never expose the `service_role` or secret key in public clients.** Prefer publishable keys for frontend code. Legacy `anon` keys are only for compatibility. In Next.js, any `NEXT_PUBLIC_` env var is sent to the browser.\r\n  - **Use scoped personal access tokens for the Management API, CLI, and MCP server.** A classic personal access token carries the user's full account access, on every organization and project. For scripts, CI, and agents, have the user create a scoped token limited to the organizations, projects, and permissions the task needs. The [personal access tokens guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/platform/personal-access-tokens.md) lists the permission each Management API endpoint and MCP tool requires. Look permissions up there rather than guessing.\r\n\r\n- **RLS, views, and privileged database code**\r\n  - **Views bypass RLS by default.** In Postgres 15 and above, use `CREATE VIEW ... WITH (security_invoker = true)`. In older versions of Postgres, protect your views by revoking access from the `anon` and `authenticated` roles, or by putting them in an unexposed schema.\r\n  - **UPDATE requires a SELECT policy.** In Postgres RLS, an UPDATE needs to first SELECT the row. Without a SELECT policy, updates silently return 0 rows â€” no error, just no change.\r\n  - **`auth.role()` is deprecated â€” use the `TO` clause instead.** Supabase has deprecated `auth.role()` in favour of specifying the target role directly on the policy with `TO authenticated` or `TO anon`. Beyond deprecation, `auth.role() = 'authenticated'` breaks silently when anonymous sign-ins are enabled, because anonymous users carry the `authenticated` Postgres role and pass the check regardless of whether the user is genuinely signed in.\r\n    ```sql\r\n    -- Deprecated (do not use)\r\n    create policy \"example\" on table_name for select\r\n    using ( auth.role() = 'authenticated' );\r\n    ```\r\n  - **`TO authenticated` alone is authentication without authorization (BOLA / IDOR).** Using `TO authenticated` only checks the role â€” it does not restrict which rows a user can access. The correct pattern combines `TO authenticated` with an ownership predicate in `USING`:\r\n    ```sql\r\n    create policy \"example\" on table_name for select\r\n    to authenticated\r\n    using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );\r\n    ```\r\n  - **UPDATE policies require both `USING` and `WITH CHECK`.** Without `WITH CHECK`, a user can reassign a row's `user_id` to another user:\r\n    ```sql\r\n    create policy \"example\" on table_name for update\r\n    to authenticated\r\n    using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id )\r\n    with check ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );\r\n    ```\r\n  - **`SECURITY DEFINER` functions bypass RLS.** A `SECURITY DEFINER` function runs with its creator's privileges â€” typically a role with `bypassrls` (e.g., `postgres`). Never add `SECURITY DEFINER` to resolve a permission error; it silently removes access control without fixing the underlying cause. Prefer `SECURITY INVOKER`.\r\n  - **`SECURITY DEFINER` functions in `public` are callable by all roles.** Postgres grants `EXECUTE` to `PUBLIC` by default for every new function, so any `SECURITY DEFINER` function in `public` is a public API endpoint callable by `anon` and `authenticated` (which inherit from `PUBLIC`) without any additional grant. When `SECURITY DEFINER` is genuinely needed (e.g., bypassing RLS on an internal lookup table), keep the function in a non-exposed schema, always include an `auth.uid()` check in the function body, and run `supabase db advisors` after making changes.\r\n\r\n- **Storage access control**\r\n  - **Storage upsert requires INSERT + SELECT + UPDATE.** Granting only INSERT allows new uploads but file replacement (upsert) silently fails. You need all three.\r\n\r\n- **Dependency and supply-chain security**\r\n  - **Always pin package versions and commit lockfiles** when installing Supabase packages (`supabase-js`, `@supabase/ssr`, `supabase-py`, etc.). See the [npm security guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/security/npm-security.md) for the full checklist.\r\n\r\nFor any security concern not covered above, fetch the Supabase product security index: `https://supabase.com/docs/guides/security/product-security.md`\r\n\r\n## Supabase CLI\r\n\r\nAlways discover commands via `--help` â€” never guess. The CLI structure changes between versions.\r\n\r\n```bash\r\nsupabase --help                    # All top-level commands\r\nsupabase <group> --help            # Subcommands (e.g., supabase db --help)\r\nsupabase <group> <command> --help  # Flags for a specific command\r\n```\r\n\r\n**Supabase CLI Known gotchas:**\r\n\r\n- `supabase db query` requires **CLI v2.79.0+** â†’ use MCP `execute_sql` or `psql` as fallback\r\n- `supabase db advisors` requires **CLI v2.81.3+** â†’ use MCP `get_advisors` as fallback\r\n- The browser flow of `supabase login` creates a classic token with full account access. In CI, set `SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN` to a scoped personal access token instead. It takes precedence over any saved login. Commands that connect with the database password (`--password` or `SUPABASE_DB_PASSWORD`, for example `supabase db push`) aren't limited by the token's permissions.\r\n- In imperative migration projects, create new hand-authored migration files with `supabase migration new <name>` first. Never invent a migration filename or rely on memory for the expected format. Declarative schema projects generate migrations from `supabase/schemas/`; see \"Making and Committing Schema Changes\" below.\r\n\r\n**Version check and upgrade:** Run `supabase --version` to check. For CLI changelogs and version-specific features, consult the [CLI documentation](https://supabase.com/docs/reference/cli/introduction) or [GitHub releases](https://github.com/supabase/cli/releases).\r\n\r\n## Supabase MCP Server\r\n\r\nFor setup instructions, server URL, and configuration, see the [MCP setup guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/getting-started/mcp).\r\n\r\n**Troubleshooting connection issues** â€” follow these steps in order:\r\n\r\n1. **Check if the server is reachable:**\r\n   `curl -so /dev/null -w \"%{http_code}\" https://mcp.supabase.com/mcp`\r\n   A `401` is expected (no token) and means the server is up. Timeout or \"connection refused\" means it may be down.\r\n\r\n2. **Check `.mcp.json` configuration:**\r\n   Verify the project root has a valid `.mcp.json` with the correct server URL. If missing, create one pointing to `https://mcp.supabase.com/mcp`.\r\n\r\n3. **Authenticate the MCP server:**\r\n   If the server is reachable and `.mcp.json` is correct but tools aren't visible, the user needs to authenticate. The Supabase MCP server uses OAuth 2.1 â€” tell the user to trigger the auth flow in their agent, complete it in the browser, and reload the session.\r\n   In CI or other environments where the browser flow can't run, pass a scoped personal access token in the `Authorization: Bearer` header instead.\r\n\r\n4. **Check scoped token permissions:**\r\n   If a tool fails with \"You do not have permission to perform this action\" while using a scoped personal access token, the token lacks that tool's permission or the project is outside the token's scope. Check the tool's required permission in the [personal access tokens guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/platform/personal-access-tokens.md#mcp-tools).\r\n\r\n## Supabase Documentation\r\n\r\nBefore implementing any Supabase feature, find the relevant documentation. Use these methods in priority order:\r\n\r\n1. **MCP `search_docs` tool** (preferred â€” returns relevant snippets directly)\r\n2. **Fetch docs pages as markdown** â€” any docs page can be fetched by appending `.md` to the URL path.\r\n3. **Web search** for Supabase-specific topics when you don't know which page to look at.\r\n\r\n## Making and Committing Schema Changes\r\n\r\nFirst decide which schema workflow the project uses.\r\n\r\n### Option A: Declarative schemas\r\n\r\nUse this when `supabase/schemas/` exists or `config.toml` sets `schema_paths`. Edit the desired schema state in those files, then generate and review the migration. Do not start by hand-writing a migration. See the [Declarative database schemas guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/local-development/declarative-database-schemas).\r\n\r\n### Option B: Imperative migrations\r\n\r\nUse this when the project does not use declarative schemas.\r\n\r\n**To make schema changes, use `execute_sql` (MCP) or `supabase db query` (CLI).** These run SQL directly on the database without creating migration history entries, so you can iterate freely and generate a clean migration when ready.\r\n\r\nDo NOT use `apply_migration` to change a local database schema â€” it writes a migration history entry on every call, which means you can't iterate, and `supabase db diff` / `supabase db pull` will produce empty or conflicting diffs. If you use it, you'll be stuck with whatever SQL you passed on the first try.\r\n\r\n**When ready to commit** your changes to a migration file:\r\n\r\n1. **Run advisors** â†’ `supabase db advisors` (CLI v2.81.3+) or MCP `get_advisors`. Fix any issues.\r\n2. **Review the Security Checklist above** if your changes involve views, functions, triggers, or storage.\r\n3. **Generate the migration** â†’ `supabase db pull <descriptive-name> --local --yes`\r\n4. **Verify** â†’ `supabase migration list --local`\r\n\r\n## Debugging\r\n\r\nWhen you get an error on a Supabase-related request, for example an error code from the Supabase REST API, Postgres database, or PostgREST, an empty result, getting blocked by RLS unexpectedly, or an error from a Supabase service like Auth, Realtime, Edge Functions, or Storage, you **must** fetch Supabase's [Monitoring and Debugging](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/monitoring-and-debugging.md) documentation before diagnosing or proposing a fix, rather than working from memory. MEDIUM\r\nimpactDescription: Reduced attack surface, better audit trail\r\ntags: privileges, security, roles, permissions\r\n---\r\n\r\n## Apply Principle of Least Privilege\r\n\r\nGrant only the minimum permissions required. Never use superuser for application queries.\r\n\r\n**Incorrect (overly broad permissions):**\r\n\r\n```sql\r\n-- Application uses superuser connection\r\n-- Or grants ALL to application role\r\ngrant all privileges on all tables in schema public to app_user;\r\ngrant all privileges on all sequences in schema public to app_user;\r\n\r\n-- Any SQL injection becomes catastrophic\r\n-- drop table users; cascades to everything\r\n```\r\n\r\n**Correct (minimal, specific grants):**\r\n\r\n```sql\r\n-- Create role with no default privileges\r\ncreate role app_readonly nologin;\r\n\r\n-- Grant only SELECT on specific tables\r\ngrant usage on schema public to app_readonly;\r\ngrant select on public.products, public.categories to app_readonly;\r\n\r\n-- Create role for writes with limited scope\r\ncreate role app_writer nologin;\r\ngrant usage on schema public to app_writer;\r\ngrant select, insert, update on public.orders to app_writer;\r\ngrant usage on sequence orders_id_seq to app_writer;\r\n-- No DELETE permission\r\n\r\n-- Login role inherits from these\r\ncreate role app_user login password 'xxx';\r\ngrant app_writer to app_user;\r\n```\r\n\r\nRevoke public defaults:\r\n\r\n```sql\r\n-- Revoke default public access\r\nrevoke all on schema public from public;\r\nrevoke all on all tables in schema public from public;\r\n```\r\n\r\nReference: [Roles and Privileges](https://supabase.com/blog/postgres-roles-and-privileges)\r\n---\r\ntitle: Enable Row Level Security for Multi-Tenant Data\r\nimpact: CRITICAL\r\nimpactDescription: Database-enforced tenant isolation, prevent data leaks\r\ntags: rls, row-level-security, multi-tenant, security\r\n---\r\n\r\n## Enable Row Level Security for Multi-Tenant Data\r\n\r\nRow Level Security (RLS) enforces data access at the database level, ensuring users only see their own data.\r\n\r\n**Incorrect (application-level filtering only):**\r\n\r\n```sql\r\n-- Relying only on application to filter\r\nselect * from orders where user_id = $current_user_id;\r\n\r\n-- Bug or bypass means all data is exposed!\r\nselect * from orders;  -- Returns ALL orders\r\n```\r\n\r\n**Correct (database-enforced RLS):**\r\n\r\n```sql\r\n-- Enable RLS on the table\r\nalter table orders enable row level security;\r\n\r\n-- Create policy for users to see only their orders\r\ncreate policy orders_user_policy on orders\r\n  for all\r\n  using (user_id = current_setting('app.current_user_id')::bigint);\r\n\r\n-- Force RLS even for table owners\r\nalter table orders force row level security;\r\n\r\n-- Set user context and query\r\nset app.current_user_id = '123';\r\nselect * from orders;  -- Only returns orders for user 123\r\n```\r\n\r\nPolicy for authenticated role:\r\n\r\n```sql\r\ncreate policy orders_user_policy on orders\r\n  for all\r\n  to authenticated\r\n  using (user_id = auth.uid());\r\n```\r\n\r\nReference: [Row Level Security](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security)\r\n", "exit_code": 0, "duration": {"secs": 0, "nanos": 376313200}}, "started_at_ms": 1794689913043, "completed_at_ms": 1794689913519}}

Try a different method, check documentation, inspect the error more carefully, and review relevant logs when available. Supabase issues are not always solved by retrying the same command, and the answer is not always in the logs, but logs are often worth checking before proceeding.\\r\\n\\r\\n**4. Exposing tables to the Data API:** Depending on the user's [Data API settings](https://supabase.com/dashboard/project/<ref>/integrations/data_api/settings), newly created tables may not be automatically exposed via the Data (REST) API. If this is the case, `anon` and `authenticated` roles will need to be explicitly granted access.\\r\\n\\r\\n> Note that this is separate from RLS, which controls which _rows_ are visible once a table is accessible, not whether the table is accessible at all.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen a user reports a SQL-created table is unexpectedly inaccessible, check their Data API settings and whether the roles have been granted access via explicit `GRANT` SQL. When granting public (`anon`/`authenticated`) access, always enable RLS too. See [Exposing a Table to the Data API](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/api/securing-your-api.md) for the full setup workflow.\\r\\n\\r\\n**5. RLS in exposed schemas.**\\r\\nEnable RLS on every table in any exposed schema, which includes `public` by default. This is critical in Supabase because tables in exposed schemas can be reachable through the Data API when the `anon`/`authenticated` roles have access (see [Exposing a Table to the Data API](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/api/securing-your-api.md)). For private schemas, prefer RLS as defense in depth. After enabling RLS, create policies that match the actual access model rather than defaulting every table to the same `auth.uid()` pattern.\\r\\n\\r\\n**6. Security checklist.**\\r\\nWhen working on any Supabase task that touches auth, RLS, views, storage, or user data, run through this checklist. These are Supabase-specific security traps that silently create vulnerabilities:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Auth and session security**\\r\\n  - **Never use `user_metadata` claims in JWT-based authorization decisions.** In Supabase, `raw_user_meta_data` is user-editable and can appear in `auth.jwt()`, so it is unsafe for RLS policies or any other authorization logic. Store authorization data in `raw_app_meta_data` / `app_metadata` instead.\\r\\n  - **Deleting a user does not invalidate existing access tokens.** Sign out or revoke sessions first, keep JWT expiry short for sensitive apps, and for strict guarantees validate `session_id` against `auth.sessions` on sensitive operations.\\r\\n  - **If you use `app_metadata` or `auth.jwt()` for authorization, remember JWT claims are not always fresh until the user's token is refreshed.**\\r\\n\\r\\n- **API key and client exposure**\\r\\n  - **Never expose the `service_role` or secret key in public clients.** Prefer publishable keys for frontend code. Legacy `anon` keys are only for compatibility. In Next.js, any `NEXT_PUBLIC_` env var is sent to the browser.\\r\\n  - **Use scoped personal access tokens for the Management API, CLI, and MCP server.** A classic personal access token carries the user's full account access, on every organization and project. For scripts, CI, and agents, have the user create a scoped token limited to the organizations, projects, and permissions the task needs. The [personal access tokens guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/platform/personal-access-tokens.md) lists the permission each Management API endpoint and MCP tool requires. Look permissions up there rather than guessing.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **RLS, views, and privileged database code**\\r\\n  - **Views bypass RLS by default.** In Postgres 15 and above, use `CREATE VIEW ... WITH (security_invoker = true)`. In older versions of Postgres, protect your views by revoking access from the `anon` and `authenticated` roles, or by putting them in an unexposed schema.\\r\\n  - **UPDATE requires a SELECT policy.** In Postgres RLS, an UPDATE needs to first SELECT the row. Without a SELECT policy, updates silently return 0 rows â€” no error, just no change.\\r\\n  - **`auth.role()` is deprecated â€” use the `TO` clause instead.** Supabase has deprecated `auth.role()` in favour of specifying the target role directly on the policy with `TO authenticated` or `TO anon`. Beyond deprecation, `auth.role() = 'authenticated'` breaks silently when anonymous sign-ins are enabled, because anonymous users carry the `authenticated` Postgres role and pass the check regardless of whether the user is genuinely signed in.\\r\\n    ```sql\\r\\n    -- Deprecated (do not use)\\r\\n    create policy \\\"example\\\" on table_name for select\\r\\n    using ( auth.role() = 'authenticated' );\\r\\n    ```\\r\\n  - **`TO authenticated` alone is authentication without authorization (BOLA / IDOR).** Using `TO authenticated` only checks the role â€” it does not restrict which rows a user can access. The correct pattern combines `TO authenticated` with an ownership predicate in `USING`:\\r\\n    ```sql\\r\\n    create policy \\\"example\\\" on table_name for select\\r\\n    to authenticated\\r\\n    using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );\\r\\n    ```\\r\\n  - **UPDATE policies require both `USING` and `WITH CHECK`.** Without `WITH CHECK`, a user can reassign a row's `user_id` to another user:\\r\\n    ```sql\\r\\n    create policy \\\"example\\\" on table_name for update\\r\\n    to authenticated\\r\\n    using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id )\\r\\n    with check ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );\\r\\n    ```\\r\\n  - **`SECURITY DEFINER` functions bypass RLS.** A `SECURITY DEFINER` function runs with its creator's privileges â€” typically a role with `bypassrls` (e.g., `postgres`). Never add `SECURITY DEFINER` to resolve a permission error; it silently removes access control without fixing the underlying cause. Prefer `SECURITY INVOKER`.\\r\\n  - **`SECURITY DEFINER` functions in `public` are callable by all roles.** Postgres grants `EXECUTE` to `PUBLIC` by default for every new function, so any `SECURITY DEFINER` function in `public` is a public API endpoint callable by `anon` and `authenticated` (which inherit from `PUBLIC`) without any additional grant. When `SECURITY DEFINER` is genuinely needed (e.g., bypassing RLS on an internal lookup table), keep the function in a non-exposed schema, always include an `auth.uid()` check in the function body, and run `supabase db advisors` after making changes.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Storage access control**\\r\\n  - **Storage upsert requires INSERT + SELECT + UPDATE.** Granting only INSERT allows new uploads but file replacement (upsert) silently fails. You need all three.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Dependency and supply-chain security**\\r\\n  - **Always pin package versions and commit lockfiles** when installing Supabase packages (`supabase-js`, `@supabase/ssr`, `supabase-py`, etc.). See the [npm security guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/security/npm-security.md) for the full checklist.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor any security concern not covered above, fetch the Supabase product security index: `https://supabase.com/docs/guides/security/product-security.md`\\r\\n\\r\\n## Supabase CLI\\r\\n\\r\\nAlways discover commands via `--help` â€” never guess. The CLI structure changes between versions.\\r\\n\\r\\n```bash\\r\\nsupabase --help                    # All top-level commands\\r\\nsupabase <group> --help            # Subcommands (e.g., supabase db --help)\\r\\nsupabase <group> <command> --help  # Flags for a specific command\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**Supabase CLI Known gotchas:**\\r\\n\\r\\n- `supabase db query` requires **CLI v2.79.0+** â†’ use MCP `execute_sql` or `psql` as fallback\\r\\n- `supabase db advisors` requires **CLI v2.81.3+** â†’ use MCP `get_advisors` as fallback\\r\\n- The browser flow of `supabase login` creates a classic token with full account access. In CI, set `SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN` to a scoped personal access token instead. It takes precedence over any saved login. Commands that connect with the database password (`--password` or `SUPABASE_DB_PASSWORD`, for example `supabase db push`) aren't limited by the token's permissions.\\r\\n- In imperative migration projects, create new hand-authored migration files with `supabase migration new <name>` first. Never invent a migration filename or rely on memory for the expected format. Declarative schema projects generate migrations from `supabase/schemas/`; see \\\"Making and Committing Schema Changes\\\" below.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Version check and upgrade:** Run `supabase --version` to check. For CLI changelogs and version-specific features, consult the [CLI documentation](https://supabase.com/docs/reference/cli/introduction) or [GitHub releases](https://github.com/supabase/cli/releases).\\r\\n\\r\\n## Supabase MCP Server\\r\\n\\r\\nFor setup instructions, server URL, and configuration, see the [MCP setup guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/getting-started/mcp).\\r\\n\\r\\n**Troubleshooting connection issues** â€” follow these steps in order:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Check if the server is reachable:**\\r\\n   `curl -so /dev/null -w \\\"%{http_code}\\\" https://mcp.supabase.com/mcp`\\r\\n   A `401` is expected (no token) and means the server is up. Timeout or \\\"connection refused\\\" means it may be down.\\r\\n\\r\\n2. **Check `.mcp.json` configuration:**\\r\\n   Verify the project root has a valid `.mcp.json` with the correct server URL. If missing, create one pointing to `https://mcp.supabase.com/mcp`.\\r\\n\\r\\n3. **Authenticate the MCP server:**\\r\\n   If the server is reachable and `.mcp.json` is correct but tools aren't visible, the user needs to authenticate. The Supabase MCP server uses OAuth 2.1 â€” tell the user to trigger the auth flow in their agent, complete it in the browser, and reload the session.\\r\\n   In CI or other environments where the browser flow can't run, pass a scoped personal access token in the `Authorization: Bearer` header instead.\\r\\n\\r\\n4. **Check scoped token permissions:**\\r\\n   If a tool fails with \\\"You do not have permission to perform this action\\\" while using a scoped personal access token, the token lacks that tool's permission or the project is outside the token's scope. Check the tool's required permission in the [personal access tokens guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/platform/personal-access-tokens.md#mcp-tools).\\r\\n\\r\\n## Supabase Documentation\\r\\n\\r\\nBefore implementing any Supabase feature, find the relevant documentation. Use these methods in priority order:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **MCP `search_docs` tool** (preferred â€” returns relevant snippets directly)\\r\\n2. **Fetch docs pages as markdown** â€” any docs page can be fetched by appending `.md` to the URL path.\\r\\n3. **Web search** for Supabase-specific topics when you don't know which page to look at.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Making and Committing Schema Changes\\r\\n\\r\\nFirst decide which schema workflow the project uses.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Option A: Declarative schemas\\r\\n\\r\\nUse this when `supabase/schemas/` exists or `config.toml` sets `schema_paths`. Edit the desired schema state in those files, then generate and review the migration. Do not start by hand-writing a migration. See the [Declarative database schemas guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/local-development/declarative-database-schemas).\\r\\n\\r\\n### Option B: Imperative migrations\\r\\n\\r\\nUse this when the project does not use declarative schemas.\\r\\n\\r\\n**To make schema changes, use `execute_sql` (MCP) or `supabase db query` (CLI).** These run SQL directly on the database without creating migration history entries, so you can iterate freely and generate a clean migration when ready.\\r\\n\\r\\nDo NOT use `apply_migration` to change a local database schema â€” it writes a migration history entry on every call, which means you can't iterate, and `supabase db diff` / `supabase db pull` will produce empty or conflicting diffs. If you use it, you'll be stuck with whatever SQL you passed on the first try.\\r\\n\\r\\n**When ready to commit** your changes to a migration file:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Run advisors** â†’ `supabase db advisors` (CLI v2.81.3+) or MCP `get_advisors`. Fix any issues.\\r\\n2. **Review the Security Checklist above** if your changes involve views, functions, triggers, or storage.\\r\\n3. **Generate the migration** â†’ `supabase db pull <descriptive-name> --local --yes`\\r\\n4. **Verify** â†’ `supabase migration list --local`\\r\\n\\r\\n## Debugging\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen you get an error on a Supabase-related request, for example an error code from the Supabase REST API, Postgres database, or PostgREST, an empty result, getting blocked by RLS unexpectedly, or an error from a Supabase service like Auth, Realtime, Edge Functions, or Storage, you **must** fetch Supabase's [Monitoring and Debugging](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/monitoring-and-debugging.md) documentation before diagnosing or proposing a fix, rather than working from memory. The same docs also cover performance optimizations, such as slow queries and missing indexes.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Reference Guides\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Skill Feedback** â†’ [references/skill-feedback.md](references/skill-feedback.md)\\r\\n  **MUST read when** the user reports that this skill gave incorrect guidance or is missing information.\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: supabase-postgres-best-practices\\r\\ndescription: \\\"Postgres best practices maintained by Supabase, for Postgres running anywhere.
