Apply Principle of Least Privilege\\r\\n\\r\\nGrant only the minimum permissions required. Never use superuser for application queries.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Incorrect (overly broad permissions):**\\r\\n\\r\\n```sql\\r\\n-- Application uses superuser connection\\r\\n-- Or grants ALL to application role\\r\\ngrant all privileges on all tables in schema public to app_user;\\r\\ngrant all privileges on all sequences in schema public to app_user;\\r\\n\\r\\n-- Any SQL injection becomes catastrophic\\r\\n-- drop table users; cascades to everything\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**Correct (minimal, specific grants):**\\r\\n\\r\\n```sql\\r\\n-- Create role with no default privileges\\r\\ncreate role app_readonly nologin;\\r\\n\\r\\n-- Grant only SELECT on specific tables\\r\\ngrant usage on schema public to app_readonly;\\r\\ngrant select on public.products, public.categories to app_readonly;\\r\\n\\r\\n-- Create role for writes with limited scope\\r\\ncreate role app_writer nologin;\\r\\ngrant usage on schema public to app_writer;\\r\\ngrant select, insert, update on public.orders to app_writer;\\r\\ngrant usage on sequence orders_id_seq to app_writer;\\r\\n-- No DELETE permission\\r\\n\\r\\n-- Login role inherits from these\\r\\ncreate role app_user login password 'xxx';\\r\\ngrant app_writer to app_user;\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nRevoke public defaults:\\r\\n\\r\\n```sql\\r\\n-- Revoke default public access\\r\\nrevoke all on schema pub…8043 tokens (`alembic/`) manages all registered application models. Current core head is `0001_sprint1`. This API completion adds **no core table/column migration**. The approved 44 columns, constraints, indexes, triggers, grants and policies are unchanged.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Local commands\\r\\n\\r\\n```powershell\\r\\n& '.\\\\.venv\\\\Scripts\\\\python.exe' -m alembic current\\r\\n& '.\\\\.venv\\\\Scripts\\\\python.exe' -m alembic heads\\r\\n& '.\\\\.venv\\\\Scripts\\\\python.exe' -m alembic upgrade head\\r\\n& '.\\\\.venv\\\\Scripts\\\\python.exe' -m alembic check\\r\\n& '.\\\\.venv\\\\Scripts\\\\python.exe' -m alembic upgrade head --sql\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThe last command renders review SQL without connecting. Online commands use MIGRATION_DATABASE_URL only. Runtime never inherits it. The initial migration references existing auth.users/auth.uid and authenticated/anon roles; its local minimal Auth fixture is explicitly isolated from migration code. Never execute tests/auth_fixture.sql against an existing Supabase database.\\r\\n\\r\\nDo not use Base.metadata.create_all/drop_all, Alembic stamp, database reset, or direct schema synchronization. Migrations are reviewed, versioned changes. Downgrades delete objects/data and require appropriate authorization; the automated round-trip test is limited to the fresh test database created during the task.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Creating a module revision\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Set BACKEND_MODULES to the module package and import its models through the registry.\\r\\n2. Create a revision with `python -m alembic revision --autogenerate -m 'add module records'`.\\r\\n3. Check its down_revision against current shared heads. Review generated SQL and keep migration code independent of mutable model imports.\\r\\n4. Confirm only intended public tables are changed. Auth/managed schemas must never be created/altered/dropped, even if reflected by PostgreSQL.\\r\\n5. Add/check owner FKs, indexes, nullability, defaults, validation, immutable columns, RLS/grants and any owned triggers explicitly.\\r\\n6. Upgrade/check/test on a disposable local database. Coordinate other teammates' revisions before a PR.\\r\\n\\r\\nAlembic reflection uses an explicit schema search path to preserve public/auth FK qualifications. The registry permits only owned public application tables. Standard autogeneration does not fully inspect RLS, privileges, functions or triggers; review them separately.\\r\\n\\r\\n## RLS/grant pattern\\r\\n\\r\\nExample for a module-owned table with `id`, `user_id` and `title` (replace table names/columns with the reviewed module design):\\r\\n\\r\\n```sql\\r\\nALTER TABLE public.your_module_records ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;\\r\\nREVOKE ALL ON public.your_module_records FROM PUBLIC, anon, authenticated;\\r\\nCREATE POLICY module_select_own ON public.your_module_records\\r\\n  FOR SELECT TO authenticated USING (user_id = (SELECT auth.uid()));\\r\\nCREATE POLICY module_insert_own ON public.your_module_records\\r\\n  FOR INSERT TO authenticated WITH CHECK (user_id = (SELECT auth.uid()));\\r\\nCREATE POLICY module_update_own ON public.your_module_records\\r\\n  FOR UPDATE TO authenticated\\r\\n  USING (user_id = (SELECT auth.uid())) WITH CHECK (user_id = (SELECT auth.uid()));\\r\\nCREATE POLICY module_delete_own ON public.your_module_records\\r\\n  FOR DELETE TO authenticated USING (user_id = (SELECT auth.uid()));\\r\\nGRANT SELECT, DELETE ON public.your_module_records TO authenticated;\\r\\nGRANT INSERT (user_id, title) ON public.your_module_records TO authenticated;\\r\\nGRANT UPDATE (title) ON public.your_module_records TO authenticated;\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nNo anonymous access. IDs/defaults, owners and server-managed fields are excluded from writable grants. Ordinary queries use the separate restricted LOGIN, never table-owner/postgres/service-role credentials. Security-definer functions, if justified, require a fixed safe search_path, schema-qualified references, and tightly limited execution privileges.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Supabase deployment boundary\\r\\n\\r\\nNo remote Supabase connection or migration was performed. Remote DDL is blocked by default. Only after explicit approval and review, configure independent trusted migration/runtime URLs and use:\\r\\n\\r\\n```powershell\\r\\n# Later only, after explicit approval:\\r\\n& '.\\\\.venv\\\\Scripts\\\\python.exe' -m alembic -x allow_remote_ddl=true upgrade head\\r\\n& '.\\\\.venv\\\\Scripts\\\\python.exe' -m scripts.provision_runtime --role scheduler_runtime --allow-remote\\r\\n& '.\\\\.venv\\\\Scripts\\\\python.exe' -m app.db.check\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nPrefer direct PostgreSQL or verified session-mode pooler port 5432, with verify-full TLS and trusted certificates. Transaction-pooler port 6543 is unsupported. Custom runtime-role support, migration/role-admin privileges, TLS and actual JWT signing configuration must be verified on the target project; never substitute a privileged runtime role to get around a failure. filter uses Postgres's `= ANY`. Realtime allows a maximum of 100 values for this filter.\\n\\n\\n## Receiving `old` records\\n\\nBy default, only `new` record changes are sent but if you want to receive the `old` record (previous values) whenever you `UPDATE` or `DELETE` a record, you can set the `replica identity` of your table to `full`:\\n\\n```sql\\nalter table\\n  messages replica identity full;\\n```\\n\\n<Admonition type=\\\"caution\\\">\\n  RLS policies are not applied to `DELETE` statements, because there is no way for Postgres to verify that a user has access to a deleted record. When RLS is enabled and `replica identity` is set to `full` on a table, the `old` record contains only the primary key(s).\\n</Admonition>\\n\\n\\n## Private schemas\\n\\nPostgres Changes works out of the box for tables in the `public` schema. You can listen to tables in your private schemas by granting table `SELECT` permissions to the database role found in your access token. You can run a query similar to the following:\\n\\n```sql\\ngrant select on \\\"non_private_schema\\\".\\\"some_table\\\" to authenticated;\\n```\\n\\n<Admonition type=\\\"caution\\\">\\n  We strongly encourage you to enable RLS and create policies for tables in private schemas. Otherwise, any role you grant access to will have unfettered read access to the table.\\n</Admonition>\\n\\n\\n## Custom tokens\\n\\nYou may choose to sign your own tokens to customize claims that can be checked in your RLS policies.\\n\\nYour project JWT secret is found in the [**Settings > API keys**](/dashboard/project/_/settings/api-keys) section of the Dashboard.\\n\\n<Admonition type=\\\"caution\\\">\\n  Do not expose the `service_role` token on the client because the role is authorized to bypass row-level security.\\n</Admonition>\\n\\nTo use your own JWT with Realtime make sure to set the token after instantiating the Supabase client and before connecting to a Channel.\\n\\n<Tabs scrollable size=\\\"small\\\" type=\\\"underlined\\\" defaultActiveId=\\\"js\\\" queryGroup=\\\"language\\\">\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\"js\\\" label=\\\"JavaScript\\\">\\n    ```js\\n    const { createClient } = require('@supabase/supabase-js')\\n\\n    const supabase = createClient(process.env.SUPABASE_URL, process.env.SUPABASE_KEY, {})\\n\\n    // Set your custom JWT here\\n    supabase.realtime.setAuth('your-custom-jwt')\\n\\n    const channel = supabase\\n      .channel('db-changes')\\n      .on(\\n        'postgres_changes',\\n        {\\n          event: '*',\\n          schema: 'public',\\n          table: 'messages',\\n          filter: 'body=eq.bye',\\n        },\\n        (payload) => console.log(payload)\\n      )\\n      .subscribe()\\n    ```\\n  </TabPanel>\\n\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\"dart\\\" label=\\\"Dart\\\">\\n    ```dart\\n 'public',\\n          table: 'messages',\\n          filter: PostgresChangeFilter(\\n            type: PostgresChangeFilterType.eq,\\n            column: 'body',\\n            value: 'bye',\\n          ),\\n          callback: (payload) => print(payload),\\n        )\\n        .subscribe();\\n    ```\\n  </TabPanel>\\n\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\"swift\\\" label=\\\"Swift\\\">\\n    ```swift\\n    await UpdateAction.self,\\n      schema: \\\"public\\\",\\n      table: \\\"products\\\",\\n      filter: \\\"name=in.(red, blue, yellow)\\\"\\n    )\\n\\n    await myChannel.subscribe()\\n\\n    for await generated, you can pass them to Realtime.\\n\\n<Tabs scrollable size=\\\"small\\\" type=\\\"underlined\\\" defaultActiveId=\\\"js\\\" queryGroup=\\\"language\\\">\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\"js\\\" Limitations\\n\\n\\n### Delete events are not filterable\\n\\nYou can't filter Delete events when tracking Postgres Changes. This limitation is due to the way changes are pulled from Postgres.\\n\\n\\n### Spaces in table names\\n\\nRealtime currently does not work when table names contain spaces.\\n\\n\\n### Database instance and realtime performance\\n\\nRealtime systems usually require forethought because of their scaling dynamics. For the `Postgres Changes` feature, every change event must be checked to see if the subscribed user has access. For instance, if you have 100 users subscribed to a table where you make a single insert, it will then trigger 100 \\\"reads\\\": one for each user.\\n\\nThere can be a database bottleneck which limits message throughput. If your database cannot authorize the changes rapidly enough, the changes will be delayed until you receive a timeout.\\n\\nDatabase changes are processed on a single thread to maintain the change order. That means compute upgrades don't have a large effect on the performance of Postgres change subscriptions. You can estimate the expected maximum throughput for your database below.\\n\\nIf you are using Postgres Changes at scale, you should consider using separate \\\"public\\\" table without RLS and filters. Alternatively, you can use Realtime server-side only and then re-stream the changes to your clients using a Realtime Broadcast.\\n\\nEnter your database settings to estimate the maximum throughput for your instance:\\n\\n<RealtimeLimitsEstimator />\\n\\nDon't forget to run your own benchmarks to make sure that the performance is acceptable for your use case.\\n\\nWe are making many improvements to Realtime's Postgres Changes. If you are uncertain about the performance of your use case, reach out using [Support Form](/dashboard/support/new) and we will be happy to help you. We have a team of engineers that can advise you on the best solution for your use-case.\\n\"},{\"title\":\"Postgres Roles\",\"href\":\"https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/roles\",\"content\":\"# Postgres Roles\\n\\nManaging access to your Postgres database and configuring permissions.\\n\\nPostgres manages database access permissions using the concept of roles. Generally you wouldn't use these roles for your own application - they are mostly for configuring *system access* to your database. If you want to configure *application access*, then you should use [Row Level Security](/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security) (RLS). You can also implement [Role-based Access Control](/docs/guides/api/custom-claims-and-role-based-access-control-rbac) on top of RLS.\\n\\n\\n## Users vs roles\\n\\nIn Postgres, roles can function as users or groups of users. Users are roles with login privileges, while groups (also known as role groups) are roles that don't have login privileges but can be used to manage permissions for multiple users.\\n\\n\\n## Creating roles\\n\\nYou can create a role using the `create role` command:\\n\\n```sql\\ncreate role \\\"role_name\\\";\\n```\\n\\n\\n## Creating users\\n\\nRoles and users are essentially the same in Postgres, however if you want to use password-logins for a specific role, then you can use `WITH LOGIN PASSWORD`:\\n\\n```sql\\ncreate role \\\"role_name\\\" with login password 'extremely_secure_password';\\n```\\n\\n\\n## Passwords\\n\\nYour Postgres database is the core of your Supabase project, so it's important that every role has a strong, secure password at all times. Here are some tips for creating a secure password:\\n\\n*   Use a password manager to generate it.\\n*   Make a long password (12 characters at least).\\n*   Don't use any common dictionary words.\\n*   Use both upper and lower case characters, numbers, and special symbols.\\n\\n\\n### Special symbols in passwords\\n\\nIf you use special symbols in your Postgres password, you must remember to [percent-encode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percent-encoding) your password later if using the Postgres connection string, for example, `postgresql://postgres.projectref:p%3Dword@aws-0-us-east-1.pooler.supabase.com:6543/postgres`\\n\\n\\n### Changing your project password\\n\\nWhen you created your project you were also asked to enter a password. This is the password for the `postgres` role in your database. You can update this from the Dashboard under the [Database Settings](/dashboard/project/_/database/settings) page. You should *never* give this to third-party service unless you absolutely trust them. Instead, we recommend that you create a new user for every service that you want to give access too. This will also help you with debugging - you can see every query that each role is executing in your database within `pg_stat_statements`.\\n\\nChanging the password does not result in any downtime. All connected services, such as PostgREST, PgBouncer, and other Supabase managed services, are automatically updated to use the latest password to ensure availability. However, if you have any external services connecting to the Supabase database using hardcoded username/password credentials, a manual update will be required.\\n\\n\\n## Granting permissions\\n\\nRoles can be granted various permissions on database objects using the `GRANT` command. Permissions include `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE`. You can configure access to almost any object inside your database - including tables, views, functions, and triggers.\\n\\n\\n## Revoking permissions\\n\\nPermissions can be revoked using the `REVOKE` command:\\n\\n```sql\\nREVOKE permission_type ON object_name FROM role_name;\\n```\\n\\n\\n## Role hierarchy\\n\\nRoles can be organized in a hierarchy, where one role can inherit permissions from another. This simplifies permission management, as you can define permissions at a higher level and have them automatically apply to all child roles.\\n\\n\\n### Role inheritance\\n\\nTo create a role hierarchy, you first need to create the parent and child roles. The child role will inherit permissions from its parent. Child roles can be added using the INHERIT option when creating the role:\\n\\n```sql\\ncreate role \\\"child_role_name\\\" inherit \\\"parent_role_name\\\";\\n```\\n\\n\\n### Preventing inheritance\\n\\nIn some cases, you might want to prevent a role from having a child relationship (typically superuser roles). You can prevent inheritance relations using `NOINHERIT`:\\n\\n```sql\\nalter role \\\"child_role_name\\\" noinherit;\\n```\\n\\n\\n## Supabase roles\\n\\nPostgres comes with a set of [predefined roles](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/predefined-roles.html). Supabase extends this with a default set of roles which are configured on your database when you start a new project:\\n\\n\\n### `postgres`\\n\\nThe default Postgres role. This has admin privileges.\\n\\n\\n### `anon`\\n\\nFor unauthenticated, public access. This is the role which the API (PostgREST) will use when a user *is not* logged in.\\n\\n\\n### `authenticator`\\n\\nA special role for the API (PostgREST). It has very limited access, and is used to validate a JWT and then\\n\\\"change into\\\" another role determined by the JWT verification.\\n\\n\\n### `authenticated`\\n\\nFor \\\"authenticated access.\\\" This is the role which the API (PostgREST) will use when a user *is* logged in.\\n\\n\\n### `service_role`\\n\\nFor elevated access. This role is used by the API (PostgREST) to bypass Row Level Security.\\n\\n\\n### `supabase_auth_admin`\\n\\nUsed by the Auth middleware to connect to the database and run migration. Access is scoped to the `auth` schema.\\n\\n\\n### `supabase_storage_admin`\\n\\nUsed by the Auth middleware to connect to the database and run migration. Access is scoped to the `storage` schema.\\n\\n\\n### `supabase_etl_admin`\\n\\nUsed by [Replication powered by Supabase ETL](/docs/guides/database/replication) to replicate database changes to external destinations. Has read-all access and replication privileges for change data capture, bypasses Row Level Security, and can write to the `etl` schema.\\n\\n\\n### `dashboard_user`\\n\\nFor running commands via the Supabase UI.\\n\\n\\n### `supabase_admin`\\n\\nAn internal role Supabase uses for administrative tasks, such as running upgrades and automations.\\n\\n\\n## Resources\\n\\n*   Official Postgres docs: [Database Roles](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/database-roles.html)\\n*   Official Postgres docs: [Role Membership](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/role-membership.html)\\n*   Official Postgres docs: [Function Permissions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/perm-functions.html)\\n\"}]}}}"}]}, "duration": {"secs": 1, "nanos": 239380400}}, "started_at_ms": 1794689955928, "completed_at_ms": 1794689957172}}

manages database access permissions using the concept of roles. Generally you wouldn't use these roles for your own application - they are mostly for configuring *system access* to your database. If you want to configure *application access*, then you should use [Row Level Security](/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security) (RLS). You can also implement [Role-based Access Control](/docs/guides/api/custom-claims-and-role-based-access-control-rbac) on top of RLS.\\n\\n\\n## Users vs roles\\n\\nIn Postgres, roles can function as users or groups of users. Users are roles with login privileges, while groups (also known as role groups) are roles that don't have login privileges but can be used to manage permissions for multiple users.\\n\\n\\n## Creating roles\\n\\nYou can create a role using the `create role` command:\\n\\n```sql\\ncreate role \\\"role_name\\\";\\n```\\n\\n\\n## Creating users\\n\\nRoles and users are essentially the same in Postgres, however if you want to use password-logins for a specific role, then you can use `WITH LOGIN PASSWORD`:\\n\\n```sql\\ncreate role \\\"role_name\\\" with login password 'extremely_secure_password';\\n```\\n\\n\\n## Passwords\\n\\nYour Postgres database is the core of your Supabase project, so it's important that every role has a strong, secure password at all times. Here are some tips for creating a secure password:\\n\\n*   Use a password manager to generate it.\\n*   Make a long password (12 characters at least).\\n*   Don't use any common dictionary words.\\n*   Use both upper and lower case characters, numbers, and special symbols.\\n\\n\\n### Special symbols in passwords\\n\\nIf you use special symbols in your Postgres password, you must remember to [percent-encode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percent-encoding) your password later if using the Postgres connection string, for example, `postgresql://postgres.projectref:p%3Dword@aws-0-us-east-1.pooler.supabase.com:6543/postgres`\\n\\n\\n### Changing your project password\\n\\nWhen you created your project you were also asked to enter a password. This is the password for the `postgres` role in your database. You can update this from the Dashboard under the [Database Settings](/dashboard/project/_/database/settings) page. You should *never* give this to third-party service unless you absolutely trust them. Instead, we recommend that you create a new user for every service that you want to give access too. This will also help you with debugging - you can see every query that each role is executing in your database within `pg_stat_statements`.\\n\\nChanging the password does not result in any downtime. All connected services, such as PostgREST, PgBouncer, and other Supabase managed services, are automatically updated to use the latest password to ensure availability. However, if you have any external services connecting to the Supabase database using hardcoded username/password credentials, a manual update will be required.\\n\\n\\n## Granting permissions\\n\\nRoles can be granted various permissions on database objects using the `GRANT` command. This simplifies permission management, as you can define permissions at a higher level and have them automatically apply to all child roles.\\n\\n\\n### Role inheritance\\n\\nTo create a role hierarchy, you first need to create the parent and child roles. The backend forwards passwords only to the trusted Auth origin and never persists them. Confirmation-required signup returns no session and creates no profile. Verified login creates a missing profile and retains validated username/full_name metadata; existing profile changes are never overwritten. If a requested optional username is taken, onboarding leaves it null so login remains usable; profile PATCH can choose another name and still returns 409 on conflicts.\r\n\r\nRefresh verifies the returned JWT and subject and returns rotated tokens without requiring a database transaction. This prevents database downtime from discarding a newly rotated refresh token. Signup/login and application profile writes cannot be one distributed transaction; if database onboarding is unavailable after Auth succeeds, retry login when the database recovers. Do not create or delete an Auth account to compensate.\r\n\r\nProtected routes use `SessionDep`. A token is verified before connection acquisition. A dedicated runtime LOGIN must inherit authenticated, lack superuser/BYPASSRLS/administrative memberships, and have no ownership path to any registered application table. Per transaction, only verified subject/authenticated claims enter parameterized transaction-local settings. UTC and row_security are set locally too. Owner filters supplement PostgreSQL RLS; user_id never comes from the body.\r\n\r\nFunction-scoped dependency teardown commits or rolls back before the HTTP response is sent. Commit failures therefore cannot produce successful responses. Pool return rolls back residual transactions. Pool-size-one tests verify identity cleanup after success, failure, and connection reuse. Runtime credentials remain trusted backend secrets: SQL access with those credentials must never be given to end users.\r\n\r\nThe profile insert trigger creates exactly one preferences row. Existing triggers, column grants, CHECK constraints and policies remain active. IDs, owners, timestamps, task status and event source/status are read-only. No signup trigger is added to auth.users.\r\n\r\n## Configuration and lifecycle\r\n\r\n`Settings` reads `.env` without overriding injected environment values. Runtime uses only DATABASE_URL; Alembic/role provisioning use only MIGRATION_DATABASE_URL. Actual secrets, environments, local cluster files and signing keys are ignored. Remote database URLs require verify-full TLS; remote Auth requires HTTPS. Loopback HTTP Auth is permitted only in explicitly chosen development mode. Wildcard CORS is rejected; configure exact browser origins when necessary.\r\n\r\nNo network/SQL connection is made merely to import models or build OpenAPI. Engines and Auth HTTP connections are reused, with bounded pools and timeouts. Owned resources close in application lifespan cleanup. Missing Auth configuration allows local health/docs/test development but protected APIs remain unavailable until configured.\r\n\r\nJWT verification supports ES256/RS256 signing keys. HS256 is rejected; use asymmetric keys for local Supabase too. PyJWT 2.15.1+ supplies thread-safe JWKS caching, no redirects and a 30-second unknown-key refresh cooldown; the backend does not duplicate that cache. JWT NumericDate claims must be finite numbers (not booleans/strings), and the subject must be a non-nil UUID.\r\n\r\n## Validation and performance\r\n\r\nPATCH validates the merged record, not just submitted fields. Dates/instants remain finite; timestamps require offsets and normalize to UTC. Persisted strings reject whitespace-only required values and null characters. Collection limits are 1â€“100, default 50; offsets are 0â€“1,000,000. `has_more` uses limit+1 and avoids COUNT queries. List responses load no relationships, and query-count tests show no per-item queries. Existing owner/deadline and event owner/partial recurrence indexes support common filtering. Security role checks remain constant per transaction.\r\n\r\nWeekly rules retain local dates/times, end-day offset and their own timezone. ISO weekday derives from first_date. Validation resolves first and bounded final endpoints and rejects DST gaps/folds or non-positive resolved intervals. It cannot certify every intervening/future timezone transition. Any later consumer interpreting an occurrence must resolve both endpoints with `resolve_unambiguous_local_time` and check positive duration. You build what you believe your human\r\npartner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This\r\nskill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before\r\nanything gets built.\r\n\r\nPeople often haven't finished working out what they want. When you understand the why, you make the\r\nhundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.\r\n\r\n## First: What Do You Actually Know?\r\n\r\nBefore you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and\r\nwhy?\r\n\r\n- **Everything that matters is in the request** (\"make the icon cornflower\r\n  blue\"). Say why you're asking:\r\n  what the answer would change about what you build. They want this conversation.\r\n- **They didn't:** they may not want a conversation at all. End with a\r\n  light, one-line offer to just get going instead, like\r\n  \"Or if you'd rather I just dive in, say so.\" If they take you up on\r\n  it, this skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice\r\n  (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they\r\n  asked through the normal workflow.\r\n\r\nThat's the whole message.\r\n\r\n## The Conversation\r\n\r\nAsk a question only when the answer would change what gets built and\r\nneither the request nor the project answers it. Otherwise, state your\r\ncall and your reason as a proposal they can correct, and move the work\r\nforward. Process steps are always your calls: writing things up, where\r\nfiles go, looking further, how to show something. Do them and say so.\r\nAsk one at a time. Use plain language, pitched just a little above where\r\nyour human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use process jargon.\r\nYou never need to quote this skill to your human partner.\r\n\r\nBe clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you\r\nreport what you found, give them the most important findings and offer\r\nthe rest.\r\n\r\n**Get them describing.** Until you know why they want it, ask open\r\nquestions, with no example answers attached. Their own words carry\r\nintent that your options can't. Once you know why, when a decision has\r\nchoices you can name, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off\r\nand which you'd pick. When they say \"just guess\" or \"what do you think?\",\r\npropose something concrete.\r\n\r\n**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,\r\nmaterials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and\r\nlibraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Read from how they\r\ntalk which of those choices they want to make. Someone who raises the how\r\nor asks about trade-offs wants the options with your pick. Someone who\r\ntalks about outcomes is handing you the how: make those calls and state\r\neach in a line. When there's existing work, build on what it already\r\nuses. Never read these\r\nout as questions:\r\n\r\n- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special\r\n- why now, and what success looks like to them\r\n- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even\r\n  if it technically works)\r\n- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated\r\n- current state: what exists now, what they've tried\r\n- the details they care about\r\n\r\n**Make every question specific** to their project and what they've told\r\nyou. Ask Socratically, the way a sharp colleague would: build each\r\nquestion on their last answer or on something you found, so it helps\r\nthem think through a consequence or a case they may have missed\r\n(\"Voting closes before the meeting, and two members joined this month.\r\nDoes someone who joins mid-round get a vote?\"). When the reason isn't\r\nalready plain, say what you're hoping to learn or what the answer would\r\nchange. A proposal they can correct, plus your reason for it, often\r\nbeats a question.\r\n\r\n**Do recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking further\r\nwould help, go look: deeper into their codebase or project, their own\r\nfiles and data, or the web. Say what you looked for and what you found.\r\n\r\n**Lay out the approaches.** Once you understand what they want, and\r\nbefore you write anything up, put the ways of building it in a message\r\nof its own. Come up with several real alternatives and drop the weak\r\nones, including any that work against why they want it and any the\r\nexisting work rules out. Sketch the two or three that remain concretely\r\nenough to picture, grounded in what the project actually does, with what\r\neach trades off. Recommend one and say why, then ask which way they want\r\nto go; if they've handed you the how, say you'll go with your pick\r\ninstead. When there's genuinely one sensible way, say so in that\r\nmessage and explain why the others don't fit; the design comes in the\r\nnext one. This is for how it gets built; for what they want, get them\r\ndescribing first.\r\n\r\n**Show, don't tell.** Whenever seeing would help more than reading,\r\nsketch it in text: a few lines of what they'd see. Offer the visual\r\ncompanion (below) when the look itself is theirs to decide:\r\n\r\n- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign\r\n- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule\r\n- a flow or a sequence of steps\r\n- options that would look different from each other\r\n- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map\r\n\r\nOnce they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side\r\noptions, and throwaway prototypes they can click.\r\n\r\n**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very\r\nfast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what\r\nthey want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.\r\nWhen they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests\r\nor minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,\r\nand review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the\r\nconversation.\r\n\r\n## Play It Back\r\n\r\nPlay back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to\r\ndescribe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece\r\nbehaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to\r\nquestions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through\r\nthe whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.\r\n\r\nOnly what they said goes in as theirs. Anything you filled in goes in\r\nas your proposal, with your reason. End each chunk by asking what's wrong\r\nor missing.\r\n\r\nBefore you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll\r\nlook at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, put a\r\ntext sketch next to the description. If the look itself is theirs to\r\ndecide and they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the\r\noffer instead (its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next\r\nmessage. Once they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.\r\n\r\n## Size the Work\r\n\r\nOnce you understand what they want and they've picked an approach, say\r\nhow big the work is in plain words. They can override it.\r\n\r\n| Size | The design doc |\r\n|------|----------------|\r\n| A small change | a short one: what you already covered together, written down |\r\n| A project | the full written design (below) |\r\n\r\nShort or full, the design doc has an **Approaches** part: the two or\r\nthree ways you considered building it, what each trades off, which one\r\nthey picked, and why. They pick in the conversation, before you write\r\nthe doc.\r\n\r\nIf it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.\r\n\r\nIf this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an\r\norder, and brainstorm them one at a time.\r\n\r\n## The Written Design\r\n\r\nWrite a plain document a talented builder in the domain could plan\r\nfrom without going back to your human partner. Cover:\r\n\r\n- intent and the why\r\n- goals, non-goals, anti-goals\r\n- constraints\r\n- approaches (above)\r\n- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them\r\n- what's left to the builder\r\n\r\nFor a small change, the short design covers the same points in a line\r\nor two each and goes straight to your human partner, without the\r\nbuilder check.\r\n\r\n**Where it goes:** in a software repo,\r\n`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.\r\nOtherwise, pick a sensible place and say where. Your human partner's\r\npreferences override both.\r\n\r\n**Builder check** (for a project): dispatch a fresh subagent with\r\n`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human\r\npartner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you\r\nmay come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document\r\nuntil the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:\r\n\r\n- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer\r\n  in the document.\r\n- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets\r\n  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.\r\n- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes\r\n  what gets built.\r\n\r\nBring the \"theirs\" pile in one message, most important first. Update the\r\ndocument with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the\r\ncalls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only\r\nround of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the\r\ndocument as that builder yourself.\r\n\r\n<HARD-GATE>\r\nNothing gets built until your human partner approves the design doc:\r\nthe short one for a small change, the full one for a project.\r\nBuilding includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing\r\ndependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.\r\nReading and exploring are fine.\r\n\r\nTwo exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done\r\nand the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it\r\nstays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request\r\nthat comes back through this gate.\r\n\r\nAfter the design doc is approved, the next step is the plan: invoke\r\nsuperpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.\r\n</HARD-GATE>\r\n\r\n## Red Flags\r\n\r\n| Thought | Reality |\r\n|---------|---------|\r\n| \"I'll offer a menu of what they might want\" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |\r\n| \"I'll fill in sensible defaults\" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |\r\n| \"I've answered their questions, so I'll write the doc\" | Lay out the approaches first, in a message of their own (or, when nothing was open from the start, in your first message's short design). |\r\n| \"I should explain the process first\" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |\r\n| \"They said 'sounds good' to the idea\" | Approval covers what you showed them. A design doc you haven't written isn't approved. |\r\n| \"The spike works, I'll keep building on it\" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |\r\n\r\n## Visual Companion\r\n\r\nA browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a\r\ntool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the\r\nbrowser.\r\n\r\n**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments\r\nabove comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing\r\nelse in it:\r\n\r\n> \"This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?\"\r\n\r\nIf they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.\r\n\r\n**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**\r\nMockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.\r\nRequirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A\r\nquestion about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.\r\n\r\nIf they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before\r\nstarting the server.\r\n---\r\nname: test-driven-development\r\ndescription: Use when implementing any feature or bugfix, before writing implementation code\r\n---\r\n\r\n# Test-Driven Development (TDD)\r\n\r\n## Overview\r\n\r\nWrite the test first. Watch it fail. Write minimal code to pass.\r\n\r\n**Core principle:** If you didn't watch the test fail, you don't know if it tests the right thing.\r\n\r\n**Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**\r\n\r\n## When to Use\r\n\r\n**Always:**\r\n- New features\r\n- Bug fixes\r\n- Refactoring\r\n- Behavior changes\r\n\r\n**Exceptions (ask your human partner):**\r\n- Throwaway prototypes\r\n- Generated code\r\n- Configuration files\r\n\r\nThinking \"skip TDD just this once\"? Stop. That's rationalization.\r\n\r\n## The Iron Law\r\n\r\n```\r\nNO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST\r\n```\r\n\r\nWrite code before the test? Delete it. Start over.\r\n\r\n**No exceptions:**\r\n- Don't keep it as \"reference\"\r\n- Don't \"adapt\" it while writing tests\r\n- Don't look at it\r\n- Delete means delete\r\n\r\nImplement fresh from tests. Period.\r\n\r\n## Red-Green-Refactor\r\n\r\n```dot\r\ndigraph tdd_cycle {\r\n    rankdir=LR;\r\n    red [label=\"RED\\nWrite failing test\", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=\"#ffcccc\"];\r\n    verify_red [label=\"Verify fails\\ncorrectly\", shape=diamond];\r\n    green [label=\"GREEN\\nMinimal code\", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=\"#ccffcc\"];\r\n    verify_green [label=\"Verify passes\\nAll green\", shape=diamond];\r\n    refactor [label=\"REFACTOR\\nClean up\", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=\"#ccccff\"];\r\n    next [label=\"Next\", shape=ellipse];\r\n\r\n    red -> verify_red;\r\n    verify_red -> green [label=\"yes\"];\r\n    verify_red -> red [label=\"wrong\\nfailure\"];\r\n    green -> verify_green;\r\n    verify_green -> refactor [label=\"yes\"];\r\n    verify_green -> green [label=\"no\"];\r\n    refactor -> verify_green [label=\"stay\\ngreen\"];\r\n    verify_green -> next;\r\n    next -> red;\r\n}\r\n```\r\n\r\n### RED - Write Failing Test\r\n\r\nWrite one minimal test showing what should happen.\r\n\r\n<Good>\r\n```typescript\r\ntest('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {\r\n  let attempts = 0;\r\n  const operation = () => {\r\n    attempts++;\r\n    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');\r\n    return 'success';\r\n  };\r\n\r\n  const result = await retryOperation(operation);\r\n\r\n  expect(result).toBe('success');\r\n  expect(attempts).toBe(3);\r\n});\r\n```\r\nClear name, tests real behavior, one thing\r\n</Good>\r\n\r\n<Bad>\r\n```typescript\r\ntest('retry works', async () => {\r\n  const mock = jest.fn()\r\n    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())\r\n    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())\r\n    .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');\r\n  await retryOperation(mock);\r\n  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);\r\n});\r\n```\r\nVague name, tests mock not code\r\n</Bad>\r\n\r\n**Requirements:**\r\n- One behavior\r\n- Clear name\r\n- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)\r\n\r\n### Verify RED - Watch It Fail\r\n\r\n**MANDATORY. Never skip.**\r\n\r\n```bash\r\nnpm test path/to/test.test.ts\r\n```\r\n\r\nConfirm:\r\n- Test fails (not errors)\r\n- Failure message is expected\r\n- Fails because feature missing (not typos)\r\n\r\n**Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.\r\n\r\n**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.\r\n\r\n### GREEN - Minimal Code\r\n\r\nWrite simplest code to pass the test.\r\n\r\n<Good>\r\n```typescript\r\nasync function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {\r\n  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {\r\n    try {\r\n      return await fn();\r\n    } catch (e) {\r\n      if (i === 2) throw e;\r\n    }\r\n  }\r\n  throw new Error('unreachable');\r\n}\r\n```\r\nJust enough to pass\r\n</Good>\r\n\r\n<Bad>\r\n```typescript\r\nasync function retryOperation<T>(\r\n  fn: () => Promise<T>,\r\n  options?: {\r\n    maxRetries?: number;\r\n    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';\r\n    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;\r\n  }\r\n): Promise<T> {\r\n  // YAGNI\r\n}\r\n```\r\nOver-engineered\r\n</Bad>\r\n\r\nDon't add features, refactor other code, or \"improve\" beyond the test.\r\n\r\n### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass\r\n\r\n**MANDATORY.**\r\n\r\n```bash\r\nnpm test path/to/test.test.ts\r\n```\r\n\r\nConfirm:\r\n- Test passes\r\n- Other tests still pass\r\n- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)\r\n\r\n**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.\r\n\r\n**Other tests fail?** Fix now.\r\n\r\n**\"Other tests\" means the project's suite, not just your file.** A\r\ngreen run of the test you wrote is not a green suite. Before you call\r\nthe change done, run the project's test command (bare `pytest`,\r\n`npm test`, `cargo test` â€” whatever the repo uses) even when your task\r\nnamed only one test file. A scope statement in your task bounds the\r\ndeliverable, not your verification. Any failure that run shows â€”\r\nincluding one you didn't cause â€” goes in your report by name; a red\r\ntest you watched scroll past and didn't mention is a report falsified\r\nby omission.\r\n\r\n### REFACTOR - Clean Up\r\n\r\nAfter green only:\r\n- Remove duplication\r\n- Improve names\r\n- Extract helpers\r\n\r\nKeep tests green. Don't add behavior.\r\n\r\n### Repeat\r\n\r\nNext failing test for next feature.\r\n\r\n## Good Tests\r\n\r\n| Quality | Good | Bad |\r\n|---------|------|-----|\r\n| **Minimal** | One thing. \"and\" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |\r\n| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |\r\n| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |\r\n\r\nWhen writing or changing any test, read [writing-good-tests.md](writing-good-tests.md) for the rules that keep tests honest:\r\n- Name the production change that would make the test fail â€” before writing it\r\n- Assert on real behavior, never on mock behavior\r\n- Keep test-only code in test utilities, out of production classes\r\n- Understand a dependency's side effects before mocking it\r\n\r\n## Common Rationalizations\r\n\r\n| Excuse | Reality |\r\n|--------|---------|\r\n| \"Too simple to test\" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |\r\n| \"I'll test after\" | Tests written after pass immediately â€” which proves nothing. They may test the wrong thing, test the implementation instead of the behavior, or miss the edge case you forgot. You never watched it fail, so you never proved it can catch the bug. Test-first forces that failure. |\r\n| \"Tests after achieve same goals (spirit not ritual)\" | Tests-after answer \"what does this do?\"; tests-first answer \"what should this do?\" Tests written after are biased by the code you already wrote â€” you verify the cases you remembered, not the ones you'd have discovered. Coverage without proof the tests work. |\r\n| \"Already manually tested\" | Manual testing is ad-hoc: no record of what you covered, no way to re-run it when the code changes, easy to forget cases under pressure. \"Worked when I tried it\" â‰  comprehensive. Automated tests run the same way every time. |\r\n| \"Deleting X hours is wasteful\" | Sunk cost fallacy â€” that time is already spent either way. The real choice: rewrite with TDD (high confidence) vs. keep it and bolt tests on after (low confidence, likely bugs). Keeping code you can't trust is the waste. |\r\n| \"Keep as reference, write tests first\" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |\r\n| \"Need to explore first\" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |\r\n| \"Test hard = design unclear\" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |\r\n| \"TDD will slow me down\" | TDD IS the pragmatic path: catches bugs before commit, prevents regressions, lets you refactor without fear. \"Pragmatic\" shortcuts mean debugging in production â€” slower, not faster. |\r\n| \"Manual test faster\" | Manual doesn't prove edge cases. You'll re-test every change. |\r\n| \"Existing code has no tests\" | You're improving it. Open Swagger at `http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs`, ReDoc at `/redoc`, and OpenAPI at `/openapi.json`. All private APIs require Supabase bearer access tokens. Every operation includes schemas, validation/error descriptions and examples. Exported OpenAPI lives in docs/openapi.json.\\r\\n\\r\\nTask importance is priority 1â€“5; status is UNSCHEDULED. The backend forwards passwords only to the trusted Auth origin and never persists them. Confirmation-required signup returns no session and creates no profile. Verified login creates a missing profile and retains validated username/full_name metadata; existing profile changes are never overwritten. If a requested optional username is taken, onboarding leaves it null so login remains usable; profile PATCH can choose another name and still returns 409 on conflicts.\\r\\n\\r\\nRefresh verifies the returned JWT and subject and returns rotated tokens without requiring a database transaction. This prevents database downtime from discarding a newly rotated refresh token. Signup/login and application profile writes cannot be one distributed transaction; if database onboarding is unavailable after Auth succeeds, retry login when the database recovers. Do not create or delete an Auth account to compensate.\\r\\n\\r\\nProtected routes use `SessionDep`. A token is verified before connection acquisition. A dedicated runtime LOGIN must inherit authenticated, lack superuser/BYPASSRLS/administrative memberships, and have no ownership path to any registered application table. Per transaction, only verified subject/authenticated claims enter parameterized transaction-local settings. UTC and row_security are set locally too. Owner filters supplement PostgreSQL RLS; user_id never comes from the body.\\r\\n\\r\\nFunction-scoped dependency teardown commits or rolls back before the HTTP response is sent. Commit failures therefore cannot produce successful responses. Pool return rolls back residual transactions. Pool-size-one tests verify identity cleanup after success, failure, and connection reuse. Runtime credentials remain trusted backend secrets: SQL access with those credentials must never be given to end users.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe profile insert trigger creates exactly one preferences row. Existing triggers, column grants, CHECK constraints and policies remain active. IDs, owners, timestamps, task status and event source/status are read-only. No signup trigger is added to auth.users.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Configuration and lifecycle\\r\\n\\r\\n`Settings` reads `.env` without overriding injected environment values. Runtime uses only DATABASE_URL; Alembic/role provisioning use only MIGRATION_DATABASE_URL. Actual secrets, environments, local cluster files and signing keys are ignored. Remote database URLs require verify-full TLS; remote Auth requires HTTPS. Loopback HTTP Auth is permitted only in explicitly chosen development mode. Wildcard CORS is rejected; configure exact browser origins when necessary.\\r\\n\\r\\nNo network/SQL connection is made merely to import models or build OpenAPI. Engines and Auth HTTP connections are reused, with bounded pools and timeouts. Owned resources close in application lifespan cleanup. Missing Auth configuration allows local health/docs/test development but protected APIs remain unavailable until configured.\\r\\n\\r\\nJWT verification supports ES256/RS256 signing keys. HS256 is rejected; use asymmetric keys for local Supabase too. PyJWT 2.15.1+ supplies thread-safe JWKS caching, no redirects and a 30-second unknown-key refresh cooldown; the backend does not duplicate that cache. JWT NumericDate claims must be finite numbers (not booleans/strings), and the subject must be a non-nil UUID.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Validation and performance\\r\\n\\r\\nPATCH validates the merged record, not just submitted fields. Dates/instants remain finite; timestamps require offsets and normalize to UTC. Persisted strings reject whitespace-only required values and null characters. Collection limits are 1â€“100, default 50; offsets are 0â€“1,000,000. `has_more` uses limit+1 and avoids COUNT queries. List responses load no relationships, and query-count tests show no per-item queries. Existing owner/deadline and event owner/partial recurrence indexes support common filtering. Security role checks remain constant per transaction.\\r\\n\\r\\nWeekly rules retain local dates/times, end-day offset and their own timezone. ISO weekday derives from first_date. Validation resolves first and bounded final endpoints and rejects DST gaps/folds or non-positive resolved intervals. It cannot certify every intervening/future timezone transition. Any later consumer interpreting an occurrence must resolve both endpoints with `resolve_unambiguous_local_time` and check positive duration. Editing files in other directories requires approval. Network access is restricted.\n# Escalation Requests\r\n\r\nCommands are run outside the sandbox if they are approved by the user, or match an existing rule that allows it to run unrestricted. The command string is split into independent command segments at shell control operators, including but not limited to:\r\n\r\n- Pipes: |\r\n- Logical operators: &&, ||\r\n- Command separators: ;\r\n- Subshell boundaries: (...), $(...)\r\n\r\nEach resulting segment is evaluated independently for sandbox restrictions and approval requirements.\r\n\r\nExample:\r\n\r\ngit pull | tee output.txt\r\n\r\nThis is treated as two command segments:\r\n\r\n[\"git\", \"pull\"]\r\n\r\n[\"tee\", \"output.txt\"]\r\n\r\nCommands that use more advanced shell features like redirection (>, >>, <), substitutions ($(...), ...), environment variables (FOO=bar), or wildcard patterns (*, ?) will not be evaluated against rules, to limit the scope of what an approved rule allows.\r\n\r\n## How to request escalation\r\n\r\nIMPORTANT: To request approval to execute a command that will require escalated privileges:\r\n\r\n- Provide the `sandbox_permissions` parameter with the value `\"require_escalated\"`\r\n- Include a short question asking the user if they want to allow the action in `justification` parameter. e.g. \"Do you want to download and install dependencies for this project?\"\r\n- Optionally suggest a `prefix_rule` - this will be shown to the user with an option to persist the rule approval for future sessions.\r\n\r\nIf you run a command that is important to solving the user's query, but it fails because of sandboxing or with a likely sandbox-related network error (for example DNS/host resolution, registry/index access, or dependency download failure), rerun the command with \"require_escalated\". ALWAYS proceed to use the `justification` parameter - do not message the user before requesting approval for the command.\r\n\r\n## When to request escalation\r\n\r\nWhile commands are running inside the sandbox, here are some scenarios that will require escalation outside the sandbox:\r\n\r\n- You need to run a command that writes to a directory that requires it (e.g. running tests that write to /var)\r\n- You need to run a GUI app (e.g., open/xdg-open/osascript) to open browsers or files.\r\n- If you run a command that is important to solving the user's query, but it fails because of sandboxing or with a likely sandbox-related network error (for example DNS/host resolution, registry/index access, or dependency download failure), rerun the command with `require_escalated`. ALWAYS proceed to use the `sandbox_permissions` and `justification` parameters. do not message the user before requesting approval for the command.\r\n- You are about to take a potentially destructive action such as an `rm` or `git reset` that the user did not explicitly ask for.\r\n- Be judicious with escalating, but if completing the user's request requires it, you should do so - don't try and circumvent approvals by using other tools.\r\n\r\n## prefix_rule guidance\r\n\r\nWhen choosing a `prefix_rule`, request one that will allow you to fulfill similar requests from the user in the future without re-requesting escalation. SCHEDULING INPUTS\n- Create Task.\n- Edit Task.\n- Delete Task.\n- Define Task Type (FIXED / FLEXIBLE).\n- Define Deadline.\n- Define Estimated Duration.\n- Define Task Category.\n- Define Task Importance.\n- Add Fixed Events / Commitments.\n- Store University or Work Schedule.\n\nC. DATABASE & BACKEND FOUNDATION\n- Database schema.\n- Database relationships.\n- FastAPI backend.\n- Basic REST APIs.\n- Input validation.\n- Data persistence.\n- Backend testing.\n\nDo not implement:\n- Flutter or frontend integration.\n- Energy Score business logic.\n- Attention Score business logic.\n- Decision Engine.\n- Scheduling optimization algorithms.\n- Dynamic rescheduling.\n- Other teammates' module implementations.\n\nHowever, the shared backend infrastructure must support\nother teammates adding their modules without duplicating\nor modifying the foundation.\n\n==================================================\n3. ARCHITECTURE AND DATABASE RULES\n==================================================\n\nPreserve the approved existing database design.\n\nCore application tables:\n- profiles\n- user_preferences\n- tasks\n- events\n\nImportant rules:\n\n1. Supabase auth.users remains managed by Supabase.\n   Never create a duplicate authentication/users table.\n2. profiles.id references auth.users.id.\n3. user_preferences has a one-to-one relationship with\n   profiles.\n4. tasks and events belong to a profile/user.\n5. All application tables must enforce ownership and RLS.\n6. Use one shared SQLAlchemy Base.\n7. Use one shared database engine/session infrastructure.\n8. Use one shared Alembic environment and migration history.\n9. Never create separate migration histories per module.\n10. Never modify Supabase-managed auth schema.\n11. Do not introduce duplicate business entities.\n12. Preserve the distinction between Tasks and Events.\n\nTask requirements:\n- FIXED and FLEXIBLE types.\n- Deadline can be optional when appropriate.\n- Estimated duration must be positive.\n- Category and importance must be validated.\n- Importance uses the approved 1-5 scale.\n- Fixed time constraints must be validated correctly.\n- Task status follows the approved Sprint 1 design.\n\nEvent requirements:\n- ONCE and WEEKLY recurrence.\n- Support university/work weekly timetables.\n- Validate dates and time intervals.\n- Handle local timezone and daylight saving correctly.\n- Do not implement materialized recurring occurrences\n  or exception management in Sprint 1.\n\nUse the existing approved schema and documentation\nas the source of truth. If the implementation conflicts\nwith these rules, report the conflict before changing\nthe schema.\n\n==================================================\n4. This guide discusses ways to observe and manage them resourcefully.\\n\\n\\n### Configuring Supavisor's pool size\\n\\nYou can change how many database connections Supavisor can manage by altering the pool size in the \\\"Connection pooling\\\" section of the [Database Settings](/dashboard/project/_/database/settings):\\n\\n![Connection Info and Certificate.](/docs/img/database/pool-size.png)\\n\\nThe general rule is that if you are heavily using the PostgREST database API, you should be conscientious about raising your pool size past 40% of the Database Max Connections. Otherwise, you can commit 80% to the pool. This leaves adequate room for the Authentication server and other utilities.\\n\\nThese numbers are generalizations and depends on other Supabase products that you use and the extent of their usage. The actual values depend on your concurrent peak connection usage. For instance, if you were only using 80 connections in a week period and your database max connections is set to 500, then realistically you could allocate the difference of 420 (minus a reasonable buffer) to service more demand.\\n\\n\\n## Monitoring connections\\n\\n\\n### Capturing historical usage\\n\\n\\n#### Dashboard monitoring charts\\n\\n<Image\\n  alt=\\\"Database client connections chart\\\"\\n  src={{\\n    dark: '/docs/img/database/reports/db-connections-chart-dark.png',\\n    light: '/docs/img/database/reports/db-connections-chart-light.png',\\n  }}\\n  width={2062}\\n  height={608}\\n/>\\n\\nFor Teams and Enterprise plans, Supabase provides Advanced Telemetry charts directly within the Dashboard. The `Database client connections` chart displays historical connection data broken down by connection type:\\n\\n*   **Postgres**: Direct connections from your application\\n*   **PostgREST**: Connections from the PostgREST API layer\\n*   **Reserved**: Administrative connections for Supabase services\\n*   **Auth**: Connections from Supabase Auth service\\n*   **Storage**: Connections from Supabase Storage service\\n*   **Other roles**: Miscellaneous database connections\\n\\nThis chart helps you monitor connection pool usage, identify connection leaks, and plan capacity. It also shows a reference line for your compute size's maximum connection limit.\\n\\nFor more details on using these monitoring charts, see the [Reports guide](/docs/guides/telemetry/reports#advanced-telemetry).\\n\\n\\n#### Grafana Dashboard\\n\\nSupabase offers a Grafana Dashboard that records and visualizes over 200 project metrics, including connections. It's particularly useful for determining if idle clients are hogging connection slots.\\n\\nQuery to get all live connections:\\n\\n```sql\\nSELECT\\n  pg_stat_activity.pid as connection_id,\\n pg_stat_activity\\nON pg_stat_ssl.pid = pg_stat_activity.pid;\\n```\\n\\nInterpreting the query:\\n\\n| Column             | Description                                         |\\n| Supabase changes frequently â€” verify against changelog and current docs before implementing.**\\r\\nDo not rely on training data for Supabase features. Function signatures, config.toml settings, and API conventions change between versions.\\r\\n\\r\\nFirst, fetch `https://supabase.com/changelog.md` (a lightweight summary index â€” not a heavy pull), scan for `breaking-change` tags relevant to your task, and follow the linked page for any that apply. Try a different method, check documentation, inspect the error more carefully, and review relevant logs when available. Supabase issues are not always solved by retrying the same command, and the answer is not always in the logs, but logs are often worth checking before proceeding.\\r\\n\\r\\n**4. Exposing tables to the Data API:** Depending on the user's [Data API settings](https://supabase.com/dashboard/project/<ref>/integrations/data_api/settings), newly created tables may not be automatically exposed via the Data (REST) API. When granting public (`anon`/`authenticated`) access, always enable RLS too. See [Exposing a Table to the Data API](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/api/securing-your-api.md) for the full setup workflow.\\r\\n\\r\\n**5. RLS in exposed schemas.**\\r\\nEnable RLS on every table in any exposed schema, which includes `public` by default. This is critical in Supabase because tables in exposed schemas can be reachable through the Data API when the `anon`/`authenticated` roles have access (see [Exposing a Table to the Data API](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/api/securing-your-api.md)). For private schemas, prefer RLS as defense in depth. After enabling RLS, create policies that match the actual access model rather than defaulting every table to the same `auth.uid()` pattern.\\r\\n\\r\\n**6. Security checklist.**\\r\\nWhen working on any Supabase task that touches auth, RLS, views, storage, or user data, run through this checklist. These are Supabase-specific security traps that silently create vulnerabilities:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Auth and session security**\\r\\n  - **Never use `user_metadata` claims in JWT-based authorization decisions.** In Supabase, `raw_user_meta_data` is user-editable and can appear in `auth.jwt()`, so it is unsafe for RLS policies or any other authorization logic. Store authorization data in `raw_app_meta_data` / `app_metadata` instead.\\r\\n  - **Deleting a user does not invalidate existing access tokens.** Sign out or revoke sessions first, keep JWT expiry short for sensitive apps, and for strict guarantees validate `session_id` against `auth.sessions` on sensitive operations.\\r\\n  - **If you use `app_metadata` or `auth.jwt()` for authorization, remember JWT claims are not always fresh until the user's token is refreshed.**\\r\\n\\r\\n- **API key and client exposure**\\r\\n  - **Never expose the `service_role` or secret key in public clients.** Prefer publishable keys for frontend code. Legacy `anon` keys are only for compatibility. In Next.js, any `NEXT_PUBLIC_` env var is sent to the browser.\\r\\n  - **Use scoped personal access tokens for the Management API, CLI, and MCP server.** A classic personal access token carries the user's full account access, on every organization and project. For scripts, CI, and agents, have the user create a scoped token limited to the organizations, projects, and permissions the task needs. The [personal access tokens guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/platform/personal-access-tokens.md) lists the permission each Management API endpoint and MCP tool requires. Look permissions up there rather than guessing.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **RLS, views, and privileged database code**\\r\\n  - **Views bypass RLS by default.** In Postgres 15 and above, use `CREATE VIEW ... WITH (security_invoker = true)`. In older versions of Postgres, protect your views by revoking access from the `anon` and `authenticated` roles, or by putting them in an unexposed schema.\\r\\n  - **UPDATE requires a SELECT policy.** In Postgres RLS, an UPDATE needs to first SELECT the row. Without a SELECT policy, updates silently return 0 rows â€” no error, just no change.\\r\\n  - **`auth.role()` is deprecated â€” use the `TO` clause instead.** Supabase has deprecated `auth.role()` in favour of specifying the target role directly on the policy with `TO authenticated` or `TO anon`. Beyond deprecation, `auth.role() = 'authenticated'` breaks silently when anonymous sign-ins are enabled, because anonymous users carry the `authenticated` Postgres role and pass the check regardless of whether the user is genuinely signed in.\\r\\n    ```sql\\r\\n    -- Deprecated (do not use)\\r\\n    create policy \\\"example\\\" on table_name for select\\r\\n    using ( auth.role() = 'authenticated' );\\r\\n    ```\\r\\n  - **`TO authenticated` alone is authentication without authorization (BOLA / IDOR).** Using `TO authenticated` only checks the role â€” it does not restrict which rows a user can access. The correct pattern combines `TO authenticated` with an ownership predicate in `USING`:\\r\\n    ```sql\\r\\n    create policy \\\"example\\\" on table_name for select\\r\\n    to authenticated\\r\\n    using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );\\r\\n    ```\\r\\n  - **UPDATE policies require both `USING` and `WITH CHECK`.** Without `WITH CHECK`, a user can reassign a row's `user_id` to another user:\\r\\n    ```sql\\r\\n    create policy \\\"example\\\" on table_name for update\\r\\n    to authenticated\\r\\n    using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id )\\r\\n    with check ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );\\r\\n    ```\\r\\n  - **`SECURITY DEFINER` functions bypass RLS.** A `SECURITY DEFINER` function runs with its creator's privileges â€” typically a role with `bypassrls` (e.g., `postgres`). Never add `SECURITY DEFINER` to resolve a permission error; it silently removes access control without fixing the underlying cause. Prefer `SECURITY INVOKER`.\\r\\n  - **`SECURITY DEFINER` functions in `public` are callable by all roles.** Postgres grants `EXECUTE` to `PUBLIC` by default for every new function, so any `SECURITY DEFINER` function in `public` is a public API endpoint callable by `anon` and `authenticated` (which inherit from `PUBLIC`) without any additional grant. When `SECURITY DEFINER` is genuinely needed (e.g., bypassing RLS on an internal lookup table), keep the function in a non-exposed schema, always include an `auth.uid()` check in the function body, and run `supabase db advisors` after making changes.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Storage access control**\\r\\n  - **Storage upsert requires INSERT + SELECT + UPDATE.** Granting only INSERT allows new uploads but file replacement (upsert) silently fails. You need all three.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Dependency and supply-chain security**\\r\\n  - **Always pin package versions and commit lockfiles** when installing Supabase packages (`supabase-js`, `@supabase/ssr`, `supabase-py`, etc.). See the [npm security guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/security/npm-security.md) for the full checklist.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor any security concern not covered above, fetch the Supabase product security index: `https://supabase.com/docs/guides/security/product-security.md`\\r\\n\\r\\n## Supabase CLI\\r\\n\\r\\nAlways discover commands via `--help` â€” never guess. The CLI structure changes between versions.\\r\\n\\r\\n```bash\\r\\nsupabase --help                    # All top-level commands\\r\\nsupabase <group> --help            # Subcommands (e.g., supabase db --help)\\r\\nsupabase <group> <command> --help  # Flags for a specific command\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**Supabase CLI Known gotchas:**\\r\\n\\r\\n- `supabase db query` requires **CLI v2.79.0+** â†’ use MCP `execute_sql` or `psql` as fallback\\r\\n- `supabase db advisors` requires **CLI v2.81.3+** â†’ use MCP `get_advisors` as fallback\\r\\n- The browser flow of `supabase login` creates a classic token with full account access. In CI, set `SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN` to a scoped personal access token instead. It takes precedence over any saved login. Commands that connect with the database password (`--password` or `SUPABASE_DB_PASSWORD`, for example `supabase db push`) aren't limited by the token's permissions.\\r\\n- In imperative migration projects, create new hand-authored migration files with `supabase migration new <name>` first. Never invent a migration filename or rely on memory for the expected format. Declarative schema projects generate migrations from `supabase/schemas/`; see \\\"Making and Committing Schema Changes\\\" below.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Version check and upgrade:** Run `supabase --version` to check. For CLI changelogs and version-specific features, consult the [CLI documentation](https://supabase.com/docs/reference/cli/introduction) or [GitHub releases](https://github.com/supabase/cli/releases).\\r\\n\\r\\n## Supabase MCP Server\\r\\n\\r\\nFor setup instructions, server URL, and configuration, see the [MCP setup guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/getting-started/mcp).\\r\\n\\r\\n**Troubleshooting connection issues** â€” follow these steps in order:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Check if the server is reachable:**\\r\\n   `curl -so /dev/null -w \\\"%{http_code}\\\" https://mcp.supabase.com/mcp`\\r\\n   A `401` is expected (no token) and means the server is up. Timeout or \\\"connection refused\\\" means it may be down.\\r\\n\\r\\n2. **Check `.mcp.json` configuration:**\\r\\n   Verify the project root has a valid `.mcp.json` with the correct server URL. If missing, create one pointing to `https://mcp.supabase.com/mcp`.\\r\\n\\r\\n3. **Authenticate the MCP server:**\\r\\n   If the server is reachable and `.mcp.json` is correct but tools aren't visible, the user needs to authenticate. The Supabase MCP server uses OAuth 2.1 â€” tell the user to trigger the auth flow in their agent, complete it in the browser, and reload the session.\\r\\n   In CI or other environments where the browser flow can't run, pass a scoped personal access token in the `Authorization: Bearer` header instead.\\r\\n\\r\\n4. **Check scoped token permissions:**\\r\\n   If a tool fails with \\\"You do not have permission to perform this action\\\" while using a scoped personal access token, the token lacks that tool's permission or the project is outside the token's scope. Check the tool's required permission in the [personal access tokens guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/platform/personal-access-tokens.md#mcp-tools).\\r\\n\\r\\n## Supabase Documentation\\r\\n\\r\\nBefore implementing any Supabase feature, find the relevant documentation. Use these methods in priority order:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **MCP `search_docs` tool** (preferred â€” returns relevant snippets directly)\\r\\n2. **Fetch docs pages as markdown** â€” any docs page can be fetched by appending `.md` to the URL path.\\r\\n3. **Web search** for Supabase-specific topics when you don't know which page to look at.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Making and Committing Schema Changes\\r\\n\\r\\nFirst decide which schema workflow the project uses.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Option A: Declarative schemas\\r\\n\\r\\nUse this when `supabase/schemas/` exists or `config.toml` sets `schema_paths`. Edit the desired schema state in those files, then generate and review the migration. Do not start by hand-writing a migration. See the [Declarative database schemas guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/local-development/declarative-database-schemas).\\r\\n\\r\\n### Option B: Imperative migrations\\r\\n\\r\\nUse this when the project does not use declarative schemas.\\r\\n\\r\\n**To make schema changes, use `execute_sql` (MCP) or `supabase db query` (CLI).** These run SQL directly on the database without creating migration history entries, so you can iterate freely and generate a clean migration when ready.\\r\\n\\r\\nDo NOT use `apply_migration` to change a local database schema â€” it writes a migration history entry on every call, which means you can't iterate, and `supabase db diff` / `supabase db pull` will produce empty or conflicting diffs. If you use it, you'll be stuck with whatever SQL you passed on the first try.\\r\\n\\r\\n**When ready to commit** your changes to a migration file:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Run advisors** â†’ `supabase db advisors` (CLI v2.81.3+) or MCP `get_advisors`. Fix any issues.\\r\\n2. **Review the Security Checklist above** if your changes involve views, functions, triggers, or storage.\\r\\n3. **Generate the migration** â†’ `supabase db pull <descriptive-name> --local --yes`\\r\\n4. **Verify** â†’ `supabase migration list --local`\\r\\n\\r\\n## Debugging\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen you get an error on a Supabase-related request, for example an error code from the Supabase REST API, Postgres database, or PostgREST, an empty result, getting blocked by RLS unexpectedly, or an error from a Supabase service like Auth, Realtime, Edge Functions, or Storage, you **must** fetch Supabase's [Monitoring and Debugging](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/monitoring-and-debugging.md) documentation before diagnosing or proposing a fix, rather than working from memory. The same docs also cover performance optimizations, such as slow queries and missing indexes.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Reference Guides\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Skill Feedback** â†’ [references/skill-feedback.md](references/skill-feedback.md)\\r\\n  **MUST read when** the user reports that this skill gave incorrect guidance or is missing information.\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: supabase-postgres-best-practices\\r\\ndescription: \\\"Postgres best practices maintained by Supabase, for Postgres running anywhere. Apply Principle of Least Privilege\\r\\n\\r\\nGrant only the minimum permissions required. Never use superuser for application queries.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Incorrect (overly broad permissions):**\\r\\n\\r\\n```sql\\r\\n-- Application uses superuser connection\\r\\n-- Or grants ALL to application app_readonly;\\r\\n\\r\\n-- Create role for writes with limited scope\\r\\ncreate role app_writer nologin;\\r\\ngrant usage on schema public to app_writer;\\r\\ngrant select, insert, update on password 'xxx';\\r\\ngrant app_writer to app_user;\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nRevoke public defaults:\\r\\n\\r\\n```sql\\r\\n-- Revoke default public access\\r\\nrevoke all on schema pub…8043 tokens (`alembic/`) manages all registered application models. Current core head is `0001_sprint1`. This API completion adds **no core table/column migration**. The approved 44 columns, constraints, indexes, triggers, grants and policies are unchanged.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Local commands\\r\\n\\r\\n```powershell\\r\\n& '.\\\\.venv\\\\Scripts\\\\python.exe' -m alembic current\\r\\n& '.\\\\.venv\\\\Scripts\\\\python.exe' -m alembic heads\\r\\n& '.\\\\.venv\\\\Scripts\\\\python.exe' -m alembic upgrade head\\r\\n& '.\\\\.venv\\\\Scripts\\\\python.exe' -m alembic check\\r\\n& '.\\\\.venv\\\\Scripts\\\\python.exe' -m alembic upgrade head --sql\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThe last command renders review SQL without connecting. Online commands use MIGRATION_DATABASE_URL only. Runtime never inherits it. The initial migration references existing auth.users/auth.uid and authenticated/anon roles; its local minimal Auth fixture is explicitly isolated from migration code. Never execute tests/auth_fixture.sql against an existing Supabase database.\\r\\n\\r\\nDo not use Base.metadata.create_all/drop_all, Alembic stamp, database reset, or direct schema synchronization. Migrations are reviewed, versioned changes. Downgrades delete objects/data and require appropriate authorization; the automated round-trip test is limited to the fresh test database created during the task.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Creating a module revision\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Set BACKEND_MODULES to the module package and import its models through the registry.\\r\\n2. Create a revision with `python -m alembic revision --autogenerate -m 'add module records'`.\\r\\n3. Check its down_revision against current shared heads. Review generated SQL and keep migration code independent of mutable model imports.\\r\\n4. Confirm only intended public tables are changed. Auth/managed schemas must never be created/altered/dropped, even if reflected by PostgreSQL.\\r\\n5. Add/check owner FKs, indexes, nullability, defaults, validation, immutable columns, RLS/grants and any owned triggers explicitly.\\r\\n6. Upgrade/check/test on a disposable local database. Coordinate other teammates' revisions before a PR.\\r\\n\\r\\nAlembic reflection uses an explicit schema search path to preserve public/auth FK qualifications. The registry permits only owned public application tables. Standard autogeneration does not fully inspect RLS, privileges, functions or triggers; review them separately.\\r\\n\\r\\n## RLS/grant pattern\\r\\n\\r\\nExample for a module-owned table with `id`, `user_id` and `title` (replace table names/columns with the reviewed module design):\\r\\n\\r\\n```sql\\r\\nALTER TABLE public.your_module_records ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;\\r\\nREVOKE ALL ON public.your_module_records FROM PUBLIC, anon, authenticated;\\r\\nCREATE POLICY module_select_own ON public.your_module_records\\r\\n  FOR SELECT TO authenticated USING (user_id = (SELECT auth.uid()));\\r\\nCREATE POLICY module_insert_own ON public.your_module_records\\r\\n  FOR INSERT TO authenticated WITH CHECK (user_id = (SELECT auth.uid()));\\r\\nCREATE POLICY module_update_own ON public.your_module_records\\r\\n  FOR UPDATE TO authenticated\\r\\n  USING (user_id = (SELECT auth.uid())) WITH CHECK (user_id = (SELECT auth.uid()));\\r\\nCREATE POLICY module_delete_own ON public.your_module_records\\r\\n  FOR DELETE TO authenticated USING (user_id = (SELECT auth.uid()));\\r\\nGRANT SELECT, DELETE ON public.your_module_records TO authenticated;\\r\\nGRANT INSERT (user_id, title) ON public.your_module_records TO authenticated;\\r\\nGRANT UPDATE (title) ON public.your_module_records TO authenticated;\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nNo anonymous access. IDs/defaults, owners and server-managed fields are excluded from writable grants. Ordinary queries use the separate restricted LOGIN, never table-owner/postgres/service-role credentials. Security-definer functions, if justified, require a fixed safe search_path, schema-qualified references, and tightly limited execution privileges.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Supabase deployment boundary\\r\\n\\r\\nNo remote Supabase connection or migration was performed. Remote DDL is blocked by default. Only after explicit approval and review, configure independent trusted migration/runtime URLs and use:\\r\\n\\r\\n```powershell\\r\\n# Later only, after explicit approval:\\r\\n& '.\\\\.venv\\\\Scripts\\\\python.exe' -m alembic -x allow_remote_ddl=true upgrade head\\r\\n& '.\\\\.venv\\\\Scripts\\\\python.exe' -m scripts.provision_runtime --role scheduler_runtime --allow-remote\\r\\n& '.\\\\.venv\\\\Scripts\\\\python.exe' -m app.db.check\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nPrefer direct PostgreSQL or verified session-mode pooler port 5432, with verify-full TLS and trusted certificates. Transaction-pooler port 6543 is unsupported. Custom runtime-role support, migration/role-admin privileges, TLS and actual JWT signing configuration must be verified on the target project; never substitute a privileged runtime role to get around a failure.
